entries.claim: UK consumer prices (Bank of England long-run CPI, annual averages, index 2015=100) rose from 1.28 in 1914 to 2.59 in 1918 and 3.29 in 1920: about double by the end of the war and about 2.6 times (+157%) by 1920. The annual series shows rises every year 1915-1920.
entries.plain: In Britain, everyday prices roughly doubled during the war. By 1920 they were about two and a half times what they'd been in 1914.
sources: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/CPIUKA.txt (FRED, St Louis Fed; source: Bank of England)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Annual averages from a modern reconstructed series; ratios computed by us. The official Ministry of Labour cost-of-living index of the time gave about +125% (Dec 1919) to +130% (Jan 1920) over July 1914, as reported in The Hospital, 28 Feb 1920 (seen in search results only). Gazeley (1994) argues the official index overstated wartime inflation by about 3%; Searle (2013) says wartime subsidies held the official index down while prices outside it rose. Say 'about double' and 'about two and a half times', not precise figures.

entries.claim: Wartime British unemployment was almost nil: the Bank of England series gives 0.95% (1915), 0.33% (1916), 0.47% (1917), 0.65% (1918), against 3.16% in 1914.
entries.plain: During the war, almost everyone who could work had a job. Unemployment fell below one in a hundred.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Reconstructed annual series; millions were in uniform, which is why civilian unemployment was so low. Useful hinge for the film: prices rose when the economy ran out of workers and goods, not money.

entries.claim: War finance in Britain relied heavily on monetary expansion and short-term borrowing: Treasury bills bought by banks, which the Bank of England would discount, and Treasury currency notes; an NBER chapter says the emergency measures of 1914 'set the stage for credit inflation'. About 7.9 million tons of merchant shipping were destroyed during the war.
entries.plain: The war was paid for partly with newly created money and bank credit. At the same time, submarines sank ships carrying food and materials. More money chasing fewer goods.
sources: https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c5171/c5171.pdf (NBER chapter on British war finance, seen in search summary)
entries.contested_or_simplified: The NBER detail was seen in a search summary, not read in full. Relative weight of causes (shortages vs credit) is a matter of interpretation; 'more money chasing fewer goods' is a simplification. The '40% of merchant shipping sunk' figure seen on flashcard sites is unverified; do not use.

entries.claim: In February 1915 Glasgow landlords announced a 25% rent rise. Tenants, led by the Glasgow Women's Housing Association and Mary Barbour, refused to pay; by November 1915 about 20,000 households were on rent strike. On 17 November 1915 a crowd outside the courthouse supported 49 tenants charged; charges were dropped. Parliament then passed the Increase of Rent and Mortgage Interest (War Restrictions) Act 1915 (27 November 1915), freezing rents at 1914 levels.
entries.plain: In 1915, Glasgow landlords tried to push rents up by a quarter. About twenty thousand households refused to pay. Within weeks, Parliament froze rents at pre-war levels.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Single encyclopedic source; household estimates vary 20,000-25,000. The article notes the law was weakened after 1915. Mary Barbour should appear only as a typed name card.

entries.claim: Food control: Lord Rhondda became Food Controller in 1917 and compulsory rationing of sugar (national scheme from January 1918, about half a pound a week each), then meat and butter, followed in early 1918; by 1918 official controls covered over 94% of foodstuffs, and the Food Controller bought essential supplies, with a commitment to limit price rises of basics.
entries.plain: By 1918 the government was buying most of the food and rationing sugar, meat and butter, so that scarce food was shared rather than bid up by whoever could pay most.
sources: https://everydaylivesinwar.herts.ac.uk/2015/01/food/ (University of Hertfordshire, seen in search results)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Seen via search summaries, not read in full. A Rural History (Cambridge) article argues Rhondda's success is overstated and local initiatives did much of the work. Whether controls 'held prices down' overall is unproven: the official index was propped up by subsidies (Searle 2013) while prices outside it rose. The 'shared rather than bid up' line is the film's explanation, not a source quote.

entries.claim: After the war Britain had a short boom in 1919-1920: pent-up capital was invested and shipyards took orders to replace lost tonnage. Prices kept rising: the CPI annual average rose from 2.85 (1919) to 3.29 (1920), about +15%.
entries.plain: When the war ended there was a short boom. Businesses rushed to rebuild and restock, and prices kept climbing, about fifteen percent in 1920 alone.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Percentage computed from annual averages; the peak of prices was mid/late 1920 within the year.

entries.claim: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 7% on 15 April 1920 (from 6%, set 6 November 1919). It stayed at 7% for about a year, being cut to 6% in mid-1921 and 5.5% in summer 1921 per the Bank's own chronological table.
entries.plain: In April 1920 the Bank of England pushed its interest rate up to seven percent, and held it there for about a year. Borrowing became expensive on purpose.
sources: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/-/media/boe/files/archive/ww/boe-1914-1921-vol1-introduction.pdf (Bank of England archive, 'The Bank of England 1914-1921', chronological table: '15 Bank Rate 7%' under April 1920)
https://www.bmbstaff.org.uk/bmb-staff_365.htm (seen in search: 'sudden rise in Bank Rate to 7% in April 1920, coupled with systematic cuts in public expenditure')
entries.contested_or_simplified: Exact reduction dates in 1921 were read from an OCR'd scan (first cut appears to be late April 1921); say 'about a year'. 'Dear money' is the period's term.

entries.claim: The 1920-21 slump: UK unemployment (Bank of England series) jumped from 1.95% in 1920 to 11.02% in 1921 and 9.68% in 1922; other estimates put it at 17% at the worst. Mitchell, Solomou and Weale estimate GDP fell about 22% between August 1920 and May 1921 and did not regain its 1920 level until spring 1924. In June 1921 over three million were on unemployment benefit (wholly or partly) plus over a million locked-out miners (Minister of Labour memo, CAB 24/127).
entries.plain: Then came the crash. Within a year, unemployment jumped from about two in a hundred to more than one in ten. Output fell by around a fifth.
sources: https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/education/resources/twenties-britain-part-one/unemployment-situation-1921/ (National Archives; seen in search results only, page now returns 410)
entries.contested_or_simplified: The 22% GDP fall is one estimate; the 'over three million' June 1921 figure includes part-time and the coal dispute, so use 'more than one in ten' instead. Whether the Bank Rate rise caused the slump, or only deepened a downturn already coming as the boom collapsed, is debated.

entries.claim: Prices fell after 1920: the UK CPI annual average fell from 3.29 (1920) to 3.01 (1921) and 2.58 (1922), about 22% in two years, and stayed around 2.4 through 1923-1926.
entries.plain: And prices did fall... by about a fifth in two years. Inflation was beaten. But the price was paid in jobs.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Annual averages, peak-to-trough from monthly data would be larger. Gazeley argues the official index overstated the 1920-21 fall. Wage falls in this period are not confirmed by a source we opened: put in could_not_verify.

entries.claim: The Housing, Town Planning, &c. Act 1919 (Addison Act) aimed to build 500,000 subsidised council homes in three years; only about 213,000 were built before the subsidy was scrapped amid the Geddes cuts (Wikipedia dates the end to 1922; Brian Lund, History & Policy, says subsidies ended in June 1921 once tenders for 175,000 had been approved).
entries.plain: After the war, the government promised half a million council homes. When the cuts came, only about two hundred thousand had been built.
sources: https://historyandpolicy.org/?p=1606 (History & Policy, Brian Lund, seen in search results)
https://www.insidehousing.co.uk/comment/comment/a-chance-to-celebrate-council-housings-past-present-and-future-60021 (Inside Housing, seen in search results: 213,000 of 500,000)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Date of ending differs by source (June 1921 vs 1922); say 'when the cuts came'. Strictly, the housing subsidy was halted mainly in 1921 before the Geddes report; linking it to 'the Geddes Axe' is a common simplification.

entries.claim: The Geddes Axe: the Committee on National Expenditure, chaired by Sir Eric Geddes (businessmen Inchcape, Faringdon, Maclay, Granet), appointed August 1921, reported Dec 1921-Feb 1922 recommending £87 million of economies; Cabinet adopted £52 million. Social spending (education, health, housing, pensions, unemployment) fell from £205.8m (1920-21) to £182.1m (1922-23) and £175.5m (1923-24).
entries.plain: In 1922 a committee of businessmen, led by Sir Eric Geddes, took an axe to public spending. Schools, health and housing were cut.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Single encyclopedic source; department-by-department cuts not confirmed. Geddes appears as a typed name card only.

entries.claim: In April 1925 Chancellor Winston Churchill returned sterling to the gold standard at the pre-war parity (£1 = $4.86). Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said in a 2025 speech that 'at the pre-war parity sterling was overvalued' and the burden of adjustment 'fell on domestic wages and prices', forcing deflation. Keynes opposed it (The Economic Consequences of Mr Churchill, 1925), reportedly estimating a gap of about 10%.
entries.plain: In 1925 Britain went back on gold at the old pre-war rate. Even today's Bank of England governor says the pound was set too high, so wages and prices had to be forced down to fit.
sources: https://www.bis.org/review/r250625c.pdf (BIS central bankers' speeches, Andrew Bailey 2025)
entries.contested_or_simplified: The '10%' overvaluation is Keynes's estimate reported secondhand (Dutch ESB article), not verified in his text: avoid the number. Supporters argued the move restored confidence and helped the City of London.

entries.claim: Coal and the General Strike: the Samuel Commission (report 10 March 1926) recommended a 13.5% cut in miners' wages and ending the government subsidy; mine owners also demanded longer hours. The TUC general strike ran 4-12 May 1926 with about 1.5-1.75 million workers out; the miners held out until about November and returned to longer hours, lower wages and district agreements.
entries.plain: Coal owners demanded lower pay and longer hours. In May 1926, around one and a half million workers walked out in a general strike. It lasted nine days. The miners held out for months... and lost.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The link from the gold decision to the coal wage cuts is the standard account (Keynes made it at the time) but coal's troubles had other causes too (falling export demand, Ruhr coal returning). 'Nine days' counts 4-12 May.

entries.claim: Italy's prices rose much more than Britain's: a 1920 Economist letter (Einaudi archive) reported Bachi's wholesale index up roughly eightfold versus not nearly fourfold in England (partly due to the lira's fall); a Turin working-family cost-of-living index (first half 1914 = 100) stood at 318 in January 1920 (food 351; rent held at 100). The lira fell from near par with sterling in June 1914 to 260% of par by June 1920. In 1926 it reached about 150 lire to the pound.
entries.plain: In Italy it was worse. By 1920 a working family in Turin was paying more than three times as much as before the war to live, and the lira had lost more than half its value against the pound.
sources: https://www.luigieinaudi.it/?p=3453 (Fondazione Luigi Einaudi, 'Price Movements', Einaudi's Economist correspondence)
https://luigieinaudi.it/?p=4444 (Fondazione Luigi Einaudi, seen in search)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Turin index is one city's working-family budget, not national; rents were frozen in it. Figures come from contemporary press letters via search summaries; no Istat or Banca d'Italia series confirmed.

entries.claim: In summer 1919 'caro-viveri' (cost-of-living) riots spread across Italy, notably Florence and Bologna; authorities seized stocks and fixed prices, and in places food was sold at half price; local committees ('soviets') set food-sale rules in Romagna.
entries.plain: In the summer of 1919, Italians rioted over food prices. In some towns, crowds and workers' committees forced shops to sell at half price.
sources: https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/AG19190708.2.16 (Papers Past, NZ newspaper reprinting the London Times, July 1919)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Seen in search summaries. The Papers Past link is a nice NZ angle for the user. Exact death toll not confirmed.

entries.claim: Quota 90: on 18 August 1926 at Pesaro Mussolini announced he would defend the lira; it was revalued from about 150 to the pound (1926) and pegged in December 1927 at 92.46 lire per pound (about 19 per US dollar). Finance Minister Volpi had preferred 120-125. In 1927 industrial and agricultural wages were cut by decree, by more than prices fell; reported as two cuts totalling about 20%, with real monthly industrial wages about 10% lower in 1929 than 1926 (Zamagni's estimate).
entries.plain: In 1926 Mussolini decided to push the lira's value back up, to about ninety to the pound. To make prices fit, wages were cut by government order, by around a fifth, faster than prices fell.
sources: https://pagellapolitica.it/articoli/il-pd-ha-diffuso-una-bufala-su-mussolini-che-dimezzo-gli-stipendi-delle-donne (Pagella Politica, citing Vera Zamagni, seen in search)
https://elearning.unito.it/scuolacle/mod/resource/view.php?id=74292 (University of Turin course material, seen in search)
entries.contested_or_simplified: 'About 20%' nominal cut and '~10%' real cut come from secondary summaries seen in search, not read in full. Bernardi and Ricciuti argue output costs were limited. Mussolini appears only as a typed name card.

entries.claim: Mattei's interpretation (Phenomenal World review of The Capital Order): the sharp April 1920 Bank Rate increase began Britain's deflationary turn, restored the value of creditors' loans and launched a decade of debt deflation and mass unemployment; deflation was enforced mainly by 'independent' central banks; Hawtrey, a Treasury economist, attributed inflation to rising working-class incomes.
entries.plain: Mattei argues the 1920 interest-rate jump wasn't just about prices. It made lenders' money worth more again, and it threw people out of work... and she says that was part of the point.
sources: https://uneasymoney.com/category/clara-mattei/ (David Glasner, critical blog, seen in search)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Interpretation: say 'Mattei argues'. The review paraphrases rather than quotes her. Glasner (uneasymoney) argues Hawtrey opposed both inflation and deflation and wanted only enough deflation to stabilise, and faults Mattei for not mentioning the 1918 Cunliffe report.

entries.claim: Mattei (RevDem interview, April 2023): 'the remedy for inflation lies in higher interest rates that can "cool down" the labor market'; 'unemployment serves as the best disciplinary device to suppress wages'; 'workers are blamed for the price spiral due to the fact that wages have gone up too much'; she links this to Kalecki. In The Nation (2023): 'austerity has historically never been about curbing inflation and budget control'; 'The main objective of interest rate hikes is to cool down the labor market'; 'Fewer job openings and higher unemployment diminish the bargaining power of workers.'
entries.plain: Mattei argues the usual cure for inflation, raising interest rates, works by putting people out of work. Fewer jobs means workers can't ask for more. In her words, unemployment becomes a way to keep wages down.
entries.contested_or_simplified: High confidence that she says it; it is her interpretation (with roots in Kalecki's 1943 'Political Aspects of Full Employment'). Mainstream central bankers describe rate rises as cooling demand to bring inflation down, not as discipline. Present the 'discipline' reading as hers.

entries.claim: Mattei (RevDem 2023) on recent inflation: bargaining power had 'reversed in favor of labor, and inflation is triggering further demands of social redistribution. That is exactly why austerity is hitting again, and is hitting hard.' She frames austerity as monetary (rate rises), fiscal and industrial (attacks on organised labour).
entries.plain: Mattei sees the same pattern today: when prices rise and workers start demanding more, the old cure comes back.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Her interpretation; she was speaking about 2022-23 in the US/Europe, not NZ. The school associated with 'economists who study how modern money works' (MMT) is separate from Mattei; do not merge the two in narration.

could_not_verify: UK money wages fall 1920-1922 (how far wage rates were cut after the slump): no source opened gave a figure.
The official Ministry of Labour cost-of-living index peak of about +176% over July 1914 in late 1920: not confirmed.
The 'two million unemployed' and 'prices brought down by 50% by end of 1922' figures (Lords of Finance reader note): weak source, not used.
Share of British merchant shipping sunk by U-boats (40% claim seen on flashcards only).
Keynes's 10% overvaluation estimate in his own words.
Italian national cost-of-living or CPI series 1914-1926 from Istat or Banca d'Italia; Italian money supply and deficit figures (16bn to 95bn lire debt seen only on a popular site).
Exact Italian wage-cut decree dates and percentages in 1927 (seen only in search summaries: about 20% in two steps).
Whether British rent and food controls measurably held down overall prices (official index propped by subsidies per Searle 2013).
1914-1918 Online encyclopedia articles on post-war economies of Britain and Italy were blocked (bot protection).
Exact dates of the 1921 Bank Rate cuts (OCR of Bank of England scan suggests late April 1921 to 6.5% or 6%, then 5.5% later in 1921).

entries.claim: Under the London Schedule of Payments (May 1921), German reparations were fixed at 132 billion gold marks, payable in cash and in kind (e.g. coal, timber). About 50 billion were in A and B bonds that had to be paid on schedule; the roughly 82 billion in C bonds were largely notional. Of about 3 billion gold marks due in 1922, only 435 million were paid in cash.
entries.plain: After the First World War, Germany was ordered to pay 132 billion gold marks. That meant gold, foreign money, or real goods like coal. Paper marks printed at home were no use for it.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The 132 billion headline overstates the real burden, since most of it was in C bonds historians treat as notional. Historians still disagree about how much reparations, as against domestic war debt and deficits, caused the inflation. The 'gold or foreign money' wording is our plain summary of 'gold marks plus payment in kind'. No source here states the foreign-currency requirement word for word.

entries.claim: In January 1923, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr after Germany missed reparation deliveries, chiefly coal. The Ruhr then produced roughly 80% of Germany's steel and 71% of its coal (figure from a 1936 history). Berlin declared passive resistance, which amounted to a general strike, and paid idle workers and subsidised firms, owners and workers by printing banknotes. German output fell.
entries.plain: In January 1923, French and Belgian soldiers marched into the Ruhr, Germany's coal and steel heartland. The government told workers to down tools, and kept paying them with freshly printed money. So more and more money was chasing fewer and fewer goods.
sources: https://germanhistorydocs.org/en/weimar-germany-1918-1933/ghdi:image-4161 (German History in Documents and Images, German Historical Institute)
https://www.marxists.org/archive/rosenberg/history-weimar/ch07.htm (Arthur Rosenberg, A History of the German Republic, 1936; source of the 80%/71% shares)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Inflation was already high in 1922: the mark went from about 320 to 7,400 per US dollar during that year. The Ruhr turned high inflation into hyperinflation; it did not start it. Sources give different start dates for passive resistance (19 January, February or March), and the 80%/71% shares come from a single 1936 history. No reliable figure for the fall in output was found.

entries.claim: By November 1923 one US dollar was worth about 4.2 trillion marks (4,210,500,000,000). The Reichsbank issued its first 100-trillion-mark note on 2 November 1923. Passive resistance was called off on 26 September 1923 under Chancellor Stresemann, and the Rentenmark was introduced on 16 November 1923, after which prices stabilised.
entries.plain: By November 1923, one US dollar cost more than four trillion marks. A loaf of bread cost billions. Once the strike money stopped and a new currency arrived, prices calmed down within weeks.
sources: https://historycrunch.com/ruhr-crisis/ (History Crunch, secondary; end of passive resistance on 26 Sept)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Wikipedia gives the Berlin loaf at about 200 billion marks by late 1923. 'Billions' is safe wording. Stabilisation also needed spending cuts and, later, the 1924 Dawes Plan reparations deal. Mattei-style readers note that the stabilisation was itself austerity.

entries.claim: Zimbabwe's Fast Track Land Reform Programme, from 2000, was followed by a steep fall in farm output and the economy as a whole. The IMF is quoted as estimating a 40% cumulative fall in real GDP over 2000-07 and a further 14% in 2008. Secondary sources put the fall in farm output at about 50% from 2000 levels by 2008-09.
entries.plain: Before Zimbabwe's printing presses ran wild, its farms and factories had already collapsed. After chaotic land seizures from 2000, the economy shrank by around 40 percent in seven years, then shrank again in 2008.
sources: https://wcoats.blog/2009/05 (Warren Coats, former IMF official, blog quoting IMF estimates)
entries.contested_or_simplified: The output collapse is well established, but the exact percentages here come from secondary sources, not the IMF or FAO documents themselves. Drought, sanctions or credit loss, and capital flight also played a part, and how much weight each gets is disputed.

entries.claim: An IMF Working Paper (Muñoz, WP/07/98) estimates that the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe's quasi-fiscal losses (subsidised loans, multiple exchange rates and similar operations) were about 75% of GDP in 2006. Because they were financed by creating money or issuing RBZ securities, they contributed to the four-digit inflation of 2006. Hanke and Kwok (Cato Journal, 2009) estimate the monthly inflation peak in mid-November 2008 at 79.6 billion percent, with prices roughly doubling about every day.
entries.plain: As output and tax income collapsed, Zimbabwe's central bank paid the government's way with new money. By November 2008, prices were doubling roughly every day.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Hanke's figure is an estimate built from share prices traded in two markets and parallel exchange rates, because official statistics stopped in mid-2008. The '231 million percent' official figure for July 2008 could not be confirmed. Both sides of the debate agree the printing happened. They disagree on what came first: the supply collapse or the money.

entries.claim: In April 2013 the Bank of Japan launched Quantitative and Qualitative Monetary Easing, aiming to double the monetary base in two years: from ¥138 trillion at end-2012 to a target of ¥270 trillion by end-2014, or about 60% of nominal GDP according to the BIS. It aimed to reach 2% CPI inflation in about two years. BoJ Deputy Governor Uchida said in May 2024 that deflation had ended but average inflation over the period was 0.5%, 'which fell short of our 2% goal'. Inflation rose to around 3% only after the global inflation of 2022.
entries.plain: In 2013, Japan's central bank set out to double the amount of money it had created, within just two years. Then it kept going. Prices barely moved. For nearly a decade, inflation averaged about half a percent a year.
sources: https://www.boj.or.jp/en/about/press/koen_2013/ko130729a.htm (Bank of Japan, Governor Kuroda speech, July 2013)
https://www.bis.org/review/r240527d.htm (BIS central bankers' speeches: Uchida, 'Price dynamics in Japan over the past 25 years', May 2024)
entries.contested_or_simplified: The 0.5% average is Uchida's figure for the QQE period. It includes the 2014 consumption tax rise. Mainstream economists say the money mostly sat as bank reserves and that low inflation reflected entrenched expectations, an ageing population and weak demand. Monetarists say inflation would have been even lower without QQE. Economists who study how modern money works read it as proof that money creation alone does not cause inflation.

entries.claim: Japan's earlier quantitative easing (March 2001 to March 2006) switched the BoJ's target to banks' current-account balances, raising it in steps from about ¥5 trillion to ¥35 trillion by December 2004. The BoJ promised to keep it going until core CPI was stably at zero or above. Japan had deflation for about 15 years from the late 1990s, averaging about minus 0.3%.
entries.plain: Japan had tried this before. From 2001 it flooded its banks with new money for five years, and prices still kept drifting down.
sources: https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2006/10/did-quantitative-easing-by-the-bank-of-japan-work (Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Letter, 2006)
entries.contested_or_simplified: The minus 0.3% average covers the whole deflation period, not exactly 2001-06; core CPI hovered around zero during the QE years. The ¥35 trillion is a reserves target, not the whole money supply.

entries.claim: From March 2009 the Bank of England bought £895 billion of bonds through QE (£875 billion of UK government bonds and £20 billion of corporate bonds). Its last increase was announced in November 2020. UK CPI inflation was 0.0% in the year to March 2015, the lowest since the measure began in 1989, and stayed at or around 0% for most of 2015.
entries.plain: After the 2008 crash, the Bank of England created about 895 billion pounds of new money to buy bonds. Yet by 2015, UK inflation had fallen to zero, the lowest on record.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The £895 billion was built up in stages from 2009 to 2020. About £450 billion of it came in 2020, during Covid, which was followed by the 2021-23 inflation. UK CPI was not always low after 2008: it reached around 5% in 2011, partly from VAT rises and import prices. The 2015 zero was driven by falling fuel and food prices. Say 'mostly low' and do not imply a direct link to the 2015 figure.

entries.claim: The Federal Reserve's purchases from late 2008 to October 2014 grew its balance sheet about five-fold, from about $900 billion to $4.5 trillion (Journal of Economic Perspectives). Bank reserves at the Fed rose from about $14 billion to about $2.4 trillion. After the Fed adopted a 2% target in January 2012, core PCE inflation stayed below 2% from mid-2012 until March 2018.
entries.plain: America's central bank created trillions of dollars. Its balance sheet grew five times over. For years afterwards, inflation stayed below its two percent goal.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Much of the new money sat as bank reserves rather than reaching shops and wages, which is the standard explanation. Some economists argue QE did keep inflation from falling further.

entries.claim: The Bank of England's own 2012 analysis found that its asset purchases raised a wide range of asset prices, including government bonds and shares (equities by at least as much as gilts). They boosted households' financial wealth held outside pensions, but these holdings are heavily skewed: the top 5% of households held 40% of them.
entries.plain: Where did the new money show up? In the prices of things people own: shares, bonds, and, many argue, houses. The Bank of England itself found that the gains went mostly to the wealthiest households.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The BoE paper covers financial assets. House prices are not directly confirmed here; that QE pushed up house prices is a widely held view, made more cautiously through lower mortgage rates, and is unverified in this lane. The Bank also argues most people would have been worse off without QE, which is its own counterfactual judgement.

entries.claim: US federal spending was about 43.6% of GDP in 1943 and 1944. To stop this from driving up prices, the US used the Office of Price Administration (set up under the Emergency Price Control Act of 30 January 1942) to impose price controls and rationing. It also sold war bonds to the public and brought in a mass income tax with paycheck withholding. Rockoff concludes that the state can control prices despite a vast rise in demand, but only through 'drastic regimentation'.
entries.plain: In the Second World War, America spent over 40 percent of everything it produced on the war. Prices did not explode, because the government capped prices, rationed scarce goods, and asked people to lend their savings back through war bonds.
sources: https://www.independent.org/news/article.asp?id=2491 (Robert Higgs, Independent Institute, citing Rockoff's Drastic Measures)
entries.contested_or_simplified: The CPI rose about 10% in 1941, before full controls. Black markets mean the official index understates wartime price rises, and Rockoff notes the evidence on evasion is uncertain. The 'over 40%' is calendar-year federal spending to GDP, and other series differ. No confirmed figure for total CPI rise over 1941-45 was found.

entries.claim: In Britain during the Second World War, rationing was part of a package with controlled prices, subsidies and government standards. The stabilisation policy used subsidies on items in the cost-of-living index to hold it steady and to temper wage demands. Mills and Rockoff find British price controls were evaded less than American ones, which they put down to the 'degree of regimentation'. Rationing and controls were kept after 1945 to curb inflation, and were mostly lifted in the early 1950s.
entries.plain: Britain did the same, only harder. Ration books, fixed prices and subsidies on everyday food kept the official cost of living almost flat through the war.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Searle argues the index was held 'artificially' steady while prices of goods outside it rose, so 'almost flat' applies to the official index only. National Savings drives were not confirmed in this lane, and no wartime cost-of-living percentages were found.

entries.claim: US price controls lapsed at the end of June 1946. The OPA's own report says consumer prices rose 15% in the second half of 1946, as much as in the four years after general controls began in spring 1942, an annual rate of about 30% between June and December 1946. Year-on-year inflation reached about 20% by March 1947. The Council of Economic Advisers attributes this to the end of controls, supply shortages and pent-up demand.
entries.plain: When the controls came off in 1946, prices jumped. In six months they rose as much as in the whole war. Wartime savings and shortages met all at once.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Controls were briefly restored in late July 1946 and then mostly removed later that year. One reading is that controls only delayed inflation. Another is that the burst was short and settled by 1948-49 without a lasting spiral. Both are interpretations.

entries.claim: The OAPEC oil embargo of 19 October 1973 to March 1974 helped nearly quadruple the oil price, from $2.90 a barrel before the embargo to $11.65 in January 1974. In 1979, after the Iranian Revolution cut Iranian output by 4.8 million barrels a day (7% of world supply), oil prices more than doubled between April 1979 and April 1980. US CPI inflation peaked near 15% in March 1980.
entries.plain: In 1973 the price of oil nearly quadrupled in three months. In 1979 it more than doubled again. Everything that needs fuel to make or move got dearer, and inflation in America reached almost fifteen percent.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The Federal Reserve's own history says the Great Inflation (1965-82) started before the oil shocks. It blames loose Fed policy that let money grow too fast, which helped oil costs spread to other prices. It also says 1979 was driven partly by hoarding and strong demand, not only lost supply. Present oil as the trigger, not the whole story.

entries.claim: Euro area annual inflation peaked at 10.6% in October 2022 (Eurostat final figure; flash estimate 10.7%). Energy contributed 4.44 percentage points, with energy prices about 41.5% higher than a year earlier. Food, alcohol and tobacco contributed 2.74 points, so energy and food together made up about 7.2 of the 10.6 points. Coverage links the energy surge to Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
entries.plain: In late 2022, inflation in Europe passed ten percent. Two-thirds of it came straight from energy and food, after Russia invaded Ukraine.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The contributions were not checked against the Eurostat release itself. The 4.44 points count only the direct effect of energy, so the true share including knock-on costs is larger. Energy prices were already rising in 2021, before the invasion. 'Two-thirds' is a rounding of 7.18/10.6.

entries.claim: Bernanke and Blanchard (NBER Working Paper 31417, 2023) find that most of the 2021-22 US inflation surge came from shocks to prices, not wages: sharp rises in energy, food and other commodity prices, plus price spikes in sectors where supply was limited, such as cars and goods hit by supply-chain problems. Labour-market overheating contributed less at first, but its effect is more persistent. A BLS summary says overheating became more important in 2022.
entries.plain: Two of the world's best-known mainstream economists, a former head of America's central bank among them, studied the recent inflation. Most of it, they found, came from price shocks: fuel, food, and shortages of goods. Not from workers' wages.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The authors say commodity price jumps partly reflected strong overall demand, which includes pandemic spending, so 'supply versus demand' is not a clean split. They also say bringing inflation down needs labour demand and supply better balanced. This is a working paper. Others, such as Summers and some Fed staff, gave more weight to too much demand from pandemic stimulus.

entries.claim: An IMF Working Paper (Hansen, Toscani and Zhou, WP/23/131, June 2023) finds that rising profits accounted for 45% of the average change in the euro area consumption deflator over 2022Q1-2023Q1, import prices for 40%, and labour costs for the remainder. The authors note the limited data does not point to a widespread rise in markups. The ECB said in 2023 that unit profits had 'contributed decisively' to inflation, and in 2024 that unit-profit growth peaked at 9.4% in late 2022.
entries.plain: In Europe, the IMF found that business profits made up almost half of the price rises in 2022, more than wages did. Companies passed on higher costs, and then some.
entries.contested_or_simplified: This is an accounting breakdown, not proof that firms 'caused' the inflation; profits rose partly because firms passed on energy costs. Some campaigners call it 'greedflation', which goes beyond the paper. Labour costs made up roughly 15%. 'Then some' is our interpretation and should be dropped if strict accuracy is needed.

entries.claim: An IMF Working Paper (Alvarez, Bluedorn, Hansen, Huang, Pugacheva and Sollaci, 'Wage-Price Spirals: What is the Historical Evidence?', WP/22/221, November 2022) looked at 79 episodes of rising prices and wages in advanced economies since the 1960s. Only a small minority were followed by sustained acceleration. Inflation and wage growth usually stabilised, and where real wages had fallen, they tended to catch up.
entries.plain: And the fear that wages chase prices in an endless spiral? The IMF looked back over sixty years. It found that real spirals are rare. Usually, things settle down, and wages slowly catch up.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The paper says 'small minority', not 'rare', but 'rare' is a fair plain version. The 1970s are among the exceptions, so the finding is not absolute. The paper treats a spiral as a mechanical definition and does not say how a policy response, such as rate rises, affected the outcomes.

entries.claim: New Zealand's annual consumer price inflation (Stats NZ CPI) peaked at 7.3% in the year to the June 2022 quarter, up from 6.9% in the March 2022 quarter; quarterly rise 1.7%. It was the fastest annual rise since the June 1990 quarter (7.6%), i.e. a 32-year high. Actual result.
entries.plain: By the middle of 2022, prices in New Zealand were rising seven point three percent a year. That's the fastest in thirty-two years.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Not contested. Stats NZ's own page was not opened directly; the National Tribune page republishes the Stats NZ release. 'Fastest since 1990', not an all-time record.

entries.claim: In the June 2022 quarter, Stats NZ said the 7.3% was driven mainly by construction of new homes and rents. Petrol was up 32% over the year (largest annual rise since the June 1985 quarter) and diesel up 74%; the cost of building a new dwelling was up about 18% year on year (Stats NZ citing supply-chain problems, labour costs and higher demand); rents up 4.3%.
entries.plain: What went up? Petrol, by about a third in a year. The cost of building a new house, up nearly a fifth. And rents.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Exact construction figure seen only as 'about 18%' (an 18.3% figure is unconfirmed). Food figure for that quarter not found. Petrol prices were driven mainly by world oil prices after Russia's invasion of Ukraine (not researched here in detail).

entries.claim: Stats NZ splits CPI into tradables (mostly imported or internationally priced) and non-tradables (domestic). In the December 2022 quarter: CPI 7.2%, tradables 8.2%, non-tradables 6.6%. Non-tradables had already hit 6.0% in the March 2022 quarter, then the highest since the series began in June 2000.
entries.plain: Statistics New Zealand splits price rises into two piles: things we trade with the world, like fuel... and things made and priced here, like rents and building. At the end of 2022, both piles were rising fast. Imported prices about eight percent. Home-grown prices more than six.
entries.contested_or_simplified: 'Tradables' is not identical to 'imported' - it includes goods priced on world markets, including some NZ-made. Plain version simplifies. Whether 6.6% was the series record is not explicitly confirmed.

entries.claim: Annual CPI inflation returned inside the Reserve Bank's 1-3% target band in the September 2024 quarter (2.2%, down from 3.3% in June 2024) - the first time since the March 2021 quarter. Rents (+4.5%) were the biggest contributor; council rates rose 12.2% (largest since 1990); petrol fell 8.0%, vegetables 17.9%. Westpac attributed the fall largely to a sharp fall in imported prices, with domestic inflation easing more gradually.
entries.plain: It took until late 2024 for inflation to get back inside the Reserve Bank's target of one to three percent. And it was falling import prices, like petrol, that did most of the work. Prices made here came down more slowly.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The 'imported prices did most of the work' line is Westpac's interpretation, consistent with the Stats NZ breakdown.

entries.claim: Latest CPI before 12 October 2026: annual inflation 4.1% in the year to the June 2026 quarter (up from 3.1% in March 2026), quarterly rise 1.5%. Petrol up 27.5% and diesel/other vehicle fuels up 71% over the year; without fuel, CPI would have risen 2.9%. Westpac: tradables 4.9%, non-tradables 3.4%. Actual result, released July 2026. September quarter due 22 October 2026.
entries.plain: And now it's back. Prices rose four point one percent in the year to June 2026. Take fuel out... and it's two point nine. Inside the target.
sources: https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/BU2608/S00173.htm (Stats NZ producer price release confirming 1.5% CPI quarterly rise)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Stats NZ's own CPI page not opened; figures consistent across several secondary sources and the user's report. Cause of the 2026 fuel spike not researched in this lane.

entries.claim: Reserve Bank money creation: from 25 March 2020 the RBNZ bought government bonds under the Large Scale Asset Purchase (LSAP) programme, initially NZ$30bn, ceiling later raised to NZ$100bn. Purchases halted on 14 July 2021. Actual purchases: about NZ$53.5bn of government bonds (plus about NZ$1.7bn of local government bonds), between March 2020 and July 2021, paid for with newly created central bank money.
entries.plain: In 2020 the Reserve Bank created new money and used it to buy about fifty-three billion dollars of government bonds. It was allowed to go up to a hundred billion.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Bonds were bought from investors in the market, not directly from the government; the money created sits as bank reserves. Plain 'created new money' is a fair simplification but economists argue over how much this reaches spending.

entries.claim: The Funding for Lending Programme (FLP), launched December 2020, lent banks money at the Official Cash Rate for three years to cut their funding costs. Estimated size at launch about NZ$28bn; banks had borrowed NZ$19.021bn by 2 December 2022; access closed 6 December 2022.
entries.plain: It also lent banks about nineteen billion dollars, cheap, so they could lend more cheaply to us.
entries.contested_or_simplified: An NZ$18.9bn figure circulates but was not confirmed; use 'about nineteen billion'. Much of it was drawn in 2022, after rates were already rising.

entries.claim: House prices: the REINZ House Price Index rose 29.8% in the year to May 2021 and 30.6% in the year to July 2021 (then the highest annual rise since records began); 27.2% in the year to November 2021, when the national median reached a record NZ$925,000 (up 23.8%).
entries.plain: In 2021, house prices jumped about thirty percent in a single year. The fastest on record.
entries.contested_or_simplified: House prices are not in the CPI (CPI measures new-build costs and rents, not the price of existing homes). How much of the rise came from Reserve Bank money creation versus low interest rates, government spending and housing shortages is disputed; no quantified RBNZ estimate was found.

entries.claim: Unemployment fell to 3.2% in the December 2021 quarter, the lowest since the Household Labour Force Survey began in 1986. The independent review (22 Sep 2026) called this an 'unsustainable historic low'.
entries.plain: By the end of 2021, unemployment was down to three point two percent. The lowest ever recorded.
entries.contested_or_simplified: 'Lowest ever recorded' means since the series began in 1986. Calling it 'unsustainable' is the review's judgement; others would see a tight labour market as a good outcome for workers.

entries.claim: Official Cash Rate: cut to 0.25% in March 2020; first rise to 0.5% in October 2021 (a planned August 2021 rise was delayed by lockdown); a run of rises reached 5.5% on 24 May 2023 (25bp rise, vote 5-2); held at 5.5% until the first cut, to 5.25%, in August 2024.
entries.plain: Then the Reserve Bank pushed its interest rate from a quarter of a percent... up to five and a half percent, in under two years.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Exact date of the October 2021 rise (6 October) not directly confirmed on a primary page; RBNZ decisions page returned 403. Count of consecutive rises reported as 10 or 12 in different sources - avoid saying the number.

entries.claim: Recession: Stats NZ GDP fell 0.7% in the December 2022 quarter (revised) and 0.1% in the March 2023 quarter (technical recession, announced June 2023), then fell 0.3% in the September 2023 quarter and 0.1% in the December 2023 quarter (second technical recession, announced 21 March 2024). Unemployment rose to 5.1% (December 2024 quarter), 5.4% (December 2025 quarter) and 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter (a level last seen in 2015, 'decade high'). Actual results.
entries.plain: It worked the way it's meant to. The economy shrank, twice. And unemployment climbed... from three point two percent to five point six. That's tens of thousands more people out of work.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The 2023 recessions were mild technical ones and also involved cyclones (Hale, Gabrielle). 5.6% is the latest figure, not necessarily the peak. The 'tens of thousands' line needs a sourced head-count before use (not verified here). Linking job losses to rate rises is the mainstream view of how rate rises work, not disputed in direction.

entries.claim: Reserve Bank 2024-26: cuts from August 2024 took the OCR to 2.5% (October 2025, a 50bp cut) and 2.25% on 26 November 2025 (25bp, vote 5-1). In 2026 it raised the rate again: 2.5% in July 2026 and 2.75% on 2 September 2026. Next decision 28 October 2026.
entries.plain: The Reserve Bank cut its rate back to two and a quarter percent by late 2025. Now, with fuel prices up, it's raising it again.
entries.contested_or_simplified: July 2026 level (2.5%) inferred from a 'second consecutive hike' to 2.75% and a secondary blog title; consistent with the user's report (2.25% to 2.75% July-September). Whether to raise rates against a fuel-price (imported) shock is itself debated - relevant to the chapter's argument.

entries.claim: Commerce Commission grocery market study, final report 8 March 2022: competition 'not working well' for consumers; the market is a duopoly of Foodstuffs and Woolworths NZ; major retailers' average return on capital over 12% versus about 5.5% normal for grocery retailing; excess profits widely reported as about NZ$1 million a day. Government responded with a mandatory grocery code of conduct and a grocery regulator.
entries.plain: In 2022 the Commerce Commission found New Zealand's two supermarket chains were making profits more than double a normal return. About a million dollars a day more than in a properly competitive market.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The $1 million a day figure is an estimate from the draft/final study analysis as reported; a NZ$430m/year figure could not be confirmed. The study measured high profits over several years (2015-2019 data), not price gouging during the inflation spike; do not say supermarkets 'caused' the 2022 inflation. 'Greedflation' claims are contested.

entries.claim: Royal Commission of Inquiry into COVID-19 Lessons Learned, phase two report released 10 March 2026: the roughly NZ$60bn Covid Response and Recovery Fund was spread across 821 programmes, about half unrelated to the pandemic; many failed Treasury's 'timely, temporary and targeted' test; spending drove up house prices and cost of living (government release wording). The Commission's summary says the economic response 'in part' contributed to the 2020-21 house price surge and cost-of-living pressures, with international forces also significant, and left 'widening inequalities in wealth'.
entries.plain: In March 2026 a Royal Commission found about half of the government's sixty-billion-dollar Covid recovery fund wasn't really about Covid. And it said the response helped push up house prices... while world events played a big part too.
sources: https://www.health.govt.nz/system/files/2026-07/government-response-nz-royal-commission-inquiry-covid-19-lessons-learned.pdf (Government response, July 2026, cited in user's report)
entries.contested_or_simplified: 'Half' refers to programmes/spending reported in media and a government release; the full report itself was not opened. 'Drove up house prices' is strongest in the political release; the Commission's own summary says 'in part'. The fund also covered wage subsidies (supported over a million workers).

entries.claim: Independent review of the Reserve Bank's pandemic response by Athanasios Orphanides and David Archer, commissioned February 2026, released 22 September 2026: the early response was 'praiseworthy' and 'rapid', but 'the combined stimulus, while appropriate in the early stages, was too strong for too long'; the economy 'overheated to an historically extreme degree'; LSAP expanded 'beyond what was needed' and 'later contributed to excess demand'; 'it took a full year for policy to adjust'. 12 recommendations.
entries.plain: And in September 2026 an independent review of the Reserve Bank said the support from the bank and the government was right at first... but 'too strong for too long'.
sources: https://www.treasury.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2026-09/review-monetary-c19-report-t2026-1742.pdf (Treasury advice on the draft, cited in user's report)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Review is commissioned by the current government during an election year; Labour's Chris Hipkins questioned the timing. Its remit was the Reserve Bank, not the government's budget. It does not apportion inflation between demand and world supply shocks.

entries.claim: No published estimate splits New Zealand's 2021-23 inflation between government spending, Reserve Bank money creation and world prices (per the user's report research, 12 Oct 2026). Evidence on both sides: imported (tradables) inflation hit 8.2% and domestic (non-tradables) 6.6% at end-2022, while the review and Royal Commission found domestic demand was overstimulated.
entries.plain: So what caused it? Honestly... nobody has split it up. Part came from the world: oil, shipping, war. Part came from here: too much spending chasing too few builders and houses.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Absence of an estimate is hard to prove; this lane did not search exhaustively. 'Too few builders and houses' is an interpretation linking construction-cost inflation (C2-N02) to demand - consistent with Stats NZ's mention of 'higher demand', and with the chapter's 'where money is spent' hinge (also the view of the school of economists the series follows, i.e. MMT, for the record only).

entries.claim: Australia briefly: annual CPI peaked at 7.8% in the December 2022 quarter (highest since 1990). The Reserve Bank of Australia began raising its cash rate in May 2022 and reached 4.35% on 7 November 2023, 4.25 percentage points above the start (i.e. from 0.10%), its 13th rise.
entries.plain: Across the Tasman it was the same story. Australian prices peaked at seven point eight percent, and its Reserve Bank pushed rates up thirteen times.
entries.contested_or_simplified: ABS and RBA pages not opened directly; consistent across several secondary sources. 0.10% start inferred from the 4.25-point rise.

RBNZ Official Cash Rate decisions page returned HTTP 403; exact date of the first rise to 0.5% (6 October 2021) is not directly confirmed.
Exact new-dwelling construction cost rise to June 2022 (18.3%); only 'about 18%' seen.

Any quantified RBNZ or Treasury estimate of how much the LSAP raised house prices or CPI.
The full Royal Commission phase-two report and full Orphanides-Archer review text (relied on news coverage, the Commission's summary page and the government release).
Peak unemployment head-count increase ('tens of thousands more out of work') - not sourced.
Whether 6.6% non-tradables at Dec 2022 was the series record.
Cause of the 2026 fuel price spike (not researched in this lane).
The July 2026 OCR level of 2.5% is inferred, not seen on a primary page.

entries.claim: Inflation is the rate of increase in prices over a given period, most commonly measured over a year (IMF, Ceyda Oner, F&D 'Back to Basics', 30 July 2019).
entries.plain: Inflation just means prices, in general, going up over time. It's usually measured over a year.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Not contested. 'In general' matters: one price rising (e.g. petrol) is not by itself inflation, though it feeds the average.

entries.claim: New Zealand's consumers price index (CPI) measures the rate of price change of goods and services bought by New Zealand households, using a fixed 'basket' of items weighted by household spending; prices are collected from about 2,800 shops; the basket is normally reviewed every three years (the 2023 review was missed because the Household Economic Survey was paused in Covid). The index is quarterly.
entries.plain: To measure it, the statistics office fills an imaginary shopping basket with what households usually buy... food, rent, petrol, power... and checks the price of that same basket every three months.
sources: https://stats.govt.nz/topics/consumers-price-index (Stats NZ, seen in search results; page body would not render)
https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/fandd/issues/Series/Back-to-Basics/Inflation (IMF, basket kept mostly fixed, occasionally updated)
entries.contested_or_simplified: The '2,800 shops' figure came from a search summary of Stats NZ text, not a page I could open; do not put it on screen without re-checking. The basket being out of date is a criticism raised by the Reserve Bank (per interest.co.nz).

entries.claim: NZ annual CPI inflation peaked at 7.3% in the year to the June 2022 quarter, the highest since 1990 (June 1990 quarter was 7.6%). Drivers named at the time included new-house construction costs (+18%) and petrol (+32%). Actual result.
entries.plain: In 2022, prices in New Zealand rose 7.3 percent in a year... the fastest in more than thirty years.
entries.contested_or_simplified: 'Since 1990' and 'in 32 years' both used by press; 7.6% was reached in June 1990 quarter.

entries.claim: NZ annual CPI inflation was 4.1% in the year to the June 2026 quarter (released 21 July 2026), up from 3.1% in the March quarter; petrol +27.5% and diesel +71.0% over the year; excluding fuel, about 2.9%, inside the Reserve Bank's 1-3% band. Actual result.
entries.plain: This year it's back up... 4.1 percent. But take fuel out, and it's 2.9. Much of today's rise is one thing: the price of fuel.
entries.contested_or_simplified: From secondary sources citing Stats NZ; Stats NZ release page did not render. Matches the user's own report. Fuel spike attributed (Westpac) to the Middle East war.

entries.claim: Demand-pull: expansionary policies such as lower interest rates or higher government spending can push demand above what the economy can produce, causing 'demand-pull' inflation (IMF 2019).
entries.plain: The first cause is too much spending for what the economy can actually make. More money chasing the same number of things... and prices rise.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Textbook category, accepted across schools. The key words are 'above what the economy can produce'.

entries.claim: Cost-push: supply shocks such as natural disasters or high oil prices raise production costs and push prices up (IMF 2019). Blanchard and Bernanke (NBER WP 31417, June 2023) found most of the US inflation surge that began in 2021 'was the result of shocks to prices given wages' and that tight labour markets were not the primary driver, though their effects are more persistent.
entries.plain: The second cause is rising costs. When oil or power gets dearer, almost everything that's made or moved gets dearer too... whatever the government is spending.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Blanchard and Bernanke also say commodity price rises partly reflected strong demand, and fiscal policy contributed via demand for goods in limited supply. So 'costs vs demand' is a simplification; in 2021-22 both were present.

entries.claim: Isabella M. Weber and Evan Wasner (UMass Amherst, 2023, 'Sellers' Inflation, Profits and Conflict: Why can Large Firms Hike Prices in an Emergency?', Review of Keynesian Economics) argue that recent inflation was predominantly a 'sellers' inflation' with microeconomic origins: firms with market power raising prices; upstream bottlenecks and commodity prices give windfall profits, downstream firms pass on or amplify costs, then workers push back for lost real wages.
entries.plain: The third cause is newer to the debate. Economist Isabella Weber argues that in an emergency, big firms can raise prices faster than their costs... because everyone expects prices to rise anyway.
sources: https://scholarworks.umass.edu/econ_workingpaper/343/ (UMass working paper, seen in results, fetch blocked)
https://www.kucb.org/2024-06-26/one-theory-for-what-could-keep-inflation-under-control-is-price-controls (NPR, 26 June 2024, Weber: 'inflation can also be driven by firms')
entries.contested_or_simplified: Interpretation, say it as Weber's. Note: her first name is Isabella (some listings say Isabelle). Contested: critics say markups did not rise widely and profits rose because demand was strong. Journal volume/pages (ROKE 11(2)) not confirmed.

entries.claim: IMF Working Paper WP/23/131 (Hansen, Toscani, Zhou, 23 June 2023): domestic profits accounted for about 45% and import prices about 40% of the average change in the euro area consumption deflator over 2022Q1-2023Q1; 'firms have passed on more than the nominal cost shock and have fared relatively better than workers.'
entries.plain: Even the IMF found that in Europe, in 2022, rising company profits made up almost half of the rise in prices.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Euro area only, not NZ. Authors caution that limited data did not show a widespread rise in markups; an accounting split, not proof of cause. Don't say 'greed'.

entries.claim: Keynes (General Theory, 1936, p.303), quoted by Stephanie Bell (1999): 'true inflation' is reached only when 'a further increase in the quantity of effective demand produces no further increase in output' and spends itself entirely on prices; before that point, effects are 'a question of degree'. Bell notes Keynes recognised prices are likely to rise somewhat before full employment.
entries.plain: Here's the hinge. If there are idle workers and empty factories, new spending mostly gets them working... more is made, not just charged for. It's when the economy can't make any more that extra spending turns into higher prices.
sources: https://econwpa.ub.uni-muenchen.de/econ-wp/mac/papers/0004/0004031.pdf (Stephanie Bell, 'Functional Finance: What, Why, and How?', Levy WP 287, Nov 1999, opened and read)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Simplified: prices can start rising before full capacity as bottlenecks hit particular industries (Keynes says so himself). Say 'mostly' and 'tends to', not 'never'.

entries.claim: The Royal Commission on the Covid-19 response (summary report, 2026) said the 2020-21 surge in house prices was 'in part attributable to the economic response to the pandemic' (with significant international forces too) and described 'a sustained economic tail of higher inflation and living costs'.
entries.plain: And where the money goes matters. When money pours into things we can't quickly make more of... like land and houses... it mostly bids up prices. New Zealand's own Royal Commission found the pandemic response helped push up house prices.
entries.contested_or_simplified: The Commission says 'in part'; much of the house-price surge came from very low interest rates and the Reserve Bank's response, not only government spending. Land in fixed supply is the film's general point, not the Commission's wording. Note house prices themselves are not in the CPI (construction costs and rents are).

entries.claim: Abba Lerner, 'Functional Finance and the Federal Debt', Social Research 10 (1943): 38-51. First law: government should keep total spending at the level 'enough to buy the goods that can be produced by all who want to work, and yet not enough to bring inflation by demanding (at current prices) more than can be produced' (p.40), raising its spending or cutting taxes when spending is too low, and the reverse when too high. Taxes and bond sales are 'desirable... when they would otherwise spend enough to bring about inflation' (p.40).
entries.plain: Back in 1943, economist Abba Lerner put it simply. The government's job isn't to balance its books. It's to keep total spending just right... enough to employ everyone who wants to work, but not so much that it asks for more than can be made.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Quotes are via Bell, not the original article. Lerner is a forerunner of the school the series draws on (name for the record only: Modern Monetary Theory).

entries.claim: Stephanie Kelton, The Deficit Myth (2020), argues that countries with monetary sovereignty are not like households and proposes using 'inflation and real resource limits as the measuring stick for public spending' rather than budget balance; she says the real constraint is workers, materials, energy and technology, not money.
entries.plain: Economists who study how modern money works say the same today. A government that issues its own money can't run out of it. Its real limit is inflation... running out of workers, materials and machines.
sources: https://www.dissentmagazine.org/online_articles/monetary-mythbusting-an-interview-with-stephanie-kelton (Dissent interview, 2020, seen in results; fetch blocked)
https://mises.org/mises-wire/review-stephanie-keltons-deficit-myth (critical review, search result: Kelton warns too much spending hits the resource constraint and causes rising prices)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Interpretation of a school (Modern Monetary Theory, name for the record only). Critics (e.g. John Cochrane, Mises Institute) say the view underplays how hard it is to raise taxes or cut spending quickly once inflation starts. Applies only to countries that borrow in their own currency (NZ does).

entries.claim: Tools this view proposes against inflation: taxes or spending cuts to free up resources (Lerner 1943); in Weber's version, targeted measures: she calls price controls 'an emergency measure' for when no preparation was done, and proposes 'multilayered buffer stock systems' modelled on the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which buys when prices are low and releases when they rise (NPR, 26 June 2024).
entries.plain: So if prices do start rising, there are tools besides throwing people out of work: taxes to make room, spending aimed where there's slack, emergency price caps, and stockpiles of essentials like grain or fuel, bought cheap and released when prices spike.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Price controls are heavily contested; most mainstream economists warn of shortages. Weber herself treats them as last resort. Buffer stocks and price controls are Weber's proposals; she is not formally of the money school, so attribute separately.

entries.claim: Milton Friedman: 'Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon', usually traced to his 1963 lecture 'Inflation: Causes and Consequences' (same year as Friedman & Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States). The quantity theory (MV = PT) holds that if money grows faster than output, prices rise; IMF: under the quantity theory, if the money supply grows too large relative to the economy, the currency loses purchasing power.
entries.plain: The other side deserves a fair hearing. Milton Friedman famously said inflation is always and everywhere about money... too much money for the goods there are.
sources: https://www.kansascityfed.org/documents/3892/1984-S84MISHK.pdf (Kansas City Fed, Mishkin 1984 cites Friedman 1963, search result)
entries.contested_or_simplified: The quote's wording and 1963 date are well attested; the exact first occasion (lecture vs book) is unclear. Note Friedman's 'money' and the film's 'where the money is spent' are compatible: both say the problem is spending outrunning goods.

entries.claim: The simple link between money quantity and inflation has weakened: velocity 'has historically changed in unanticipated ways'; money-supply targets in the 1970s-80s gave unsatisfactory results; Friedman later said money targeting was less successful than he hoped; from the late 1980s most central banks switched to setting short-term interest rates, and inflation targeting began in New Zealand around 1990. The Bank of England (2014) states most money is created by commercial banks making loans.
entries.plain: But most central banks gave up counting money decades ago. New Zealand was first, in 1990, to target inflation directly instead. Today they watch spending against what the economy can produce... and what people expect prices to do.
sources: https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/quarterly-bulletin/2014/q1/money-creation-in-the-modern-economy (Bank of England QB 2014 Q1, search result)
entries.contested_or_simplified: Monetarists still argue money growth (e.g. US M2 in 2020-21) predicted the recent inflation; this is live debate. Wikipedia is a secondary summary; Uhlig et al. 2016 finding cited there not opened.

entries.claim: Expectations: if people and firms expect prices to rise, they build that into wages and contracts, making inflation partly self-fulfilling (IMF 2019). Powell (Jackson Hole, 26 Aug 2022): 'the public's expectations about future inflation can play an important role in setting the path of inflation over time'; in the 1970s people 'built that belief into wage and pricing decisions'.
entries.plain: Expectations matter too. If everyone expects prices to rise, shops raise prices and workers ask for more, and the expectation comes true.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Mainstream consensus; some heterodox economists doubt how much household expectations drive prices.

entries.claim: Central banks fight inflation by raising interest rates: higher lending rates raise repayments and leave households and businesses less to spend; higher rates lower asset prices and make investment less attractive (RBA). Effects take time: maximum effect estimated at one to two years (RBA). Powell (Fed, 26 Aug 2022): 'Reducing inflation is likely to require a sustained period of below-trend growth', 'very likely be some softening of labor market conditions', bringing 'some pain to households and businesses'.
entries.plain: The official cure is to raise interest rates. Mortgages cost more, people spend less, businesses hire less... and the head of America's central bank said plainly it would bring some pain, including fewer jobs.
entries.contested_or_simplified: Central banks frame job losses as an 'unfortunate cost', not a goal; critics (and Mattei) read it as the money arm of austerity, say that as Mattei's view. Rate rises do little against a cost shock like fuel (contested).

entries.claim: Reserve Bank of New Zealand raised the Official Cash Rate from 2.50% to 2.75% in September 2026 (from 2.25% before July 2026), its first hikes in about three years, while annual inflation was 4.1%; unemployment was 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter, a 10-year high. Governor Anna Breman. Actual results; further hikes are bank forecasts only.
entries.plain: And right now in New Zealand, with unemployment already at a ten-year high, the Reserve Bank is raising rates again... to fight a price rise that's mostly fuel.
sources: https://www.fbcnews.com.fj/world/new-zealand-unemployment-climbs-to-decade-high-of-5-6-in-q2/ (Reuters via FBC, cited in user's report)
entries.contested_or_simplified: RBNZ pages blocked (403); figures from news and the user's report. 'Mostly fuel' is the film's framing from 2.9% ex-fuel vs 4.1% headline; the Bank cites broader concerns (core inflation above 2% midpoint, expectations). Election 7 Nov 2026: keep it neutral.
