draft.title: Spent on what? What really causes inflation
draft.pitch: We go back inside chapter 1's 1915 shell factory and split it in two: in one, new money wakes up idle machines and makes more shells. In the other, every machine is already running flat out, so the same money only pushes the price tag up. Then we test that one rule on real cases (Japan and Britain created huge amounts of money and prices barely moved; Germany and Zimbabwe's prices exploded once production collapsed; oil in 1973 and fuel in New Zealand today raised prices with no new money involved). We finish on who pays when governments 'fight inflation', from 1920 Britain to New Zealand now. The viewer comes away knowing that whether created money raises prices depends on what it is spent on, and that the usual cure is paid for in jobs.
draft.the_one_idea: Creating money only pushes prices up when the spending chases things the economy can't make more of, so the question is always: spent on what?
draft.how_it_explains_inflation_through_chapte: Every key image comes from chapter 1. The politician and INFLATION? from its last scene open the chapter. The 1915 shell factory (chapter 1's proof that a government 'runs out of shells, not money') becomes the model for the whole explanation. The price tag and pay packet stamped in chapter 1, page 2 become the gauges we watch. Chapter 1's line 'it can run out of workers, materials and machines' becomes the rule: shells run out and then prices rise. Chapter 1's Glasgow and its kitchen table come back for the rent strike. The experts' advice to 'stop creating new money' is tested against cases. Chapter 1's 'money' part of austerity (make borrowing expensive so jobs disappear) returns as the 1920 Bank Rate rise and its dole queue. The film then brings the same pattern to New Zealand today.
draft.honest_edge: Page 2 admits it straight away: in the very factory chapter 1 praised, the war was paid for partly with created money and prices roughly doubled (C2-H01, C2-H03). Page 3 shows the second factory, where money only raises the price tag. Page 8 says plainly 'So yes... creating money can push prices up' when it chases busy workers or land, houses and oil. It gives New Zealand's own case: house prices up about 30% in 2021 (C2-N08) and the independent review calling the support 'too strong for too long' (C2-N15). Germany and Zimbabwe (page 6) also show money creation feeding hyperinflation, framed honestly as money plus collapsing production.

pages.name: The question
pages.what_is_said: Picks up chapter 1's last question, calls it fair, and says what inflation means: prices in general going up over time, usually measured over a year. It is the whole shopping basket, not one price tag. Then it heads back to the shell factory.
pages.sample_line: inflation just means prices, in general, going up over time... usually measured over a year. not one price tag. the whole shopping basket.
pages.on_screen: Parliament (101) with the politician (201) and INFLATION? still standing from chapter 1's last frame. On 'not one price tag' a single price tag flips up. On 'the whole shopping basket' the basket slides in and the tag drops onto it. The page peels on 'the shell factory'.

pages.name: Back to the shell factory
pages.what_is_said: Britain 1915: almost everyone who can work has a job and the war is paid for partly with created money. Submarines sink ships full of food and materials. By the end of the war prices have roughly doubled: more money chasing fewer goods.
pages.sample_line: by the end of the war, prices have roughly doubled. more money... chasing fewer goods.
pages.on_screen: Munitions factory (102) with the munition women (203). On 'fewer than one in a hundred' a tiny 1-in-100 counter pops up. On 'newly created money' a bundle of banknotes drops onto the money sack. On 'sinking ships' a small cargo ship tips and slides down out of frame. On 'roughly doubled' the price tag from page 1 springs up to twice its height.

pages.name: Two factories
pages.what_is_said: The hinge: in a factory with idle machines and waiting workers, new money starts the machines and more shells come out, so the price tag stays put. In a factory already running flat out, the same money can't make more shells, so buyers bid against each other and the price tag climbs.
pages.sample_line: the same money arrives... but no more shells can be made. so buyers bid against each other, and the price tag climbs.
pages.on_screen: The page splits into two small factories side by side (the small factory painting twice: one dark, one lit). Left: workers wait at the gate (206). On 'new money arrives' coins drop in, the chimney smokes, the workers slide inside and shells stack up beside a still price tag. Right: chimney already smoking. Coins drop in, no new shells appear and the price tag climbs with a paper creak.

pages.name: Things you can't make more of
pages.what_is_said: Some things can't be made more of in a hurry at all. In 1915 Glasgow landlords tried to push rents up by a quarter. About twenty thousand households refused to pay, and within weeks Parliament froze rents. By 1918 sugar, meat and butter were rationed, so scarce food was shared rather than bid up.
pages.sample_line: about twenty thousand households refused to pay... and within weeks, parliament froze rents.
pages.on_screen: New Glasgow tenement background. On 'a quarter' a landlord's notice stamped +25% slaps onto the close. On 'refused to pay' a paper banner unrolls across the windows. On 'froze rents' chapter 1's rubber stamp crashes down and the +25% tears away. On 'rationed' a ration book and a small sugar bag flip up on the kitchen table (108).
new_paintings: ration book with sugar bag (small object)

pages.name: Test one: lots of money, flat prices
pages.what_is_said: We test the rule. Japan's central bank set out to double the money it had created, and prices barely moved, about half a percent a year. Britain's central bank created hundreds of billions of pounds, and in 2015 prices weren't rising at all. The new money pushed up the prices of things people own, shares and bonds, and the gains went mostly to the wealthiest.
pages.sample_line: the new money went into things people own... shares and bonds. and the gains went mostly to the wealthiest.
pages.on_screen: New Tokyo shop counter background. A stack of yen notes grows taller and taller while a price tag on a bowl of noodles stays still. Page peel to the bank object: money flows out past the shopping basket (its tag unchanged) and piles up around a small share-price board, which climbs.

pages.name: Test two: when production collapses
pages.what_is_said: The opposite case. In 1923 foreign soldiers marched into Germany's coal and steel heartland. Workers downed tools and the government kept paying them with newly created money: the money kept coming while coal and steel stopped. By November a US dollar cost more than four trillion marks. In Zimbabwe, years later, farms and factories collapsed first, and then the new money came.
pages.sample_line: money keeps coming... coal and steel stop. by november, one us dollar costs more than four trillion marks.
pages.on_screen: Pithead background with soldiers (reused) sliding in on 'foreign soldiers'. The pit wheel stops and the chimney goes cold on 'down tools'. On 'newly created money' notes pour onto a wheelbarrow. On 'four trillion' a 100-trillion-mark note rises up. On 'Zimbabwe' the farmland plot flips to a dry, empty field, then a cascade of notes drops.

pages.name: Test three: costs, not money
pages.what_is_said: Sometimes it isn't money at all. In 1973 the price of oil nearly quadrupled in three months, and everything made or moved with fuel got dearer. In New Zealand, prices rose 4.1% in the year to June; take fuel out and it's 2.9%.
pages.sample_line: here, prices rose four point one percent in the year to june. take fuel out... and it's two point nine.
pages.on_screen: An oil barrel crashes in with dust on '1973'. Its price tag flips from 2.90 to 11.65, and a row of price tags behind it tips up like dominoes on 'got dearer'. Page peel to a modern NZ street with a petrol pump. On 'take fuel out' the pump folds flat and the big 4.1 tag shrinks to 2.9.
new_paintings: modern New Zealand street with petrol station (background)

pages.name: The honest edge
pages.what_is_said: So yes, creating money can push prices up when the spending chases workers who are already busy, or things we can't make more of, like land, houses and oil. In 2021 New Zealand house prices jumped about thirty percent in a year. An independent review says the support from the government and the Reserve Bank was right at first, but too strong for too long.
pages.sample_line: so yes... creating money can push prices up. when the spending chases workers who are already busy, or things we can't make more of.
pages.on_screen: Back on the right-hand 'flat out' factory from page 3 for a beat. Then the farmland plot, a small house and the oil barrel flip up in a row on 'land, houses and oil'. On 'thirty percent' the house rises on its pop-up and its tag jumps. On 'too strong for too long' the royal commission report drops in and chapter 1's rubber stamp crashes onto it.

pages.name: Who pays to fight it
pages.what_is_said: How do governments fight inflation? In April 1920 the Bank of England pushed its interest rate up to seven percent. Within a year unemployment jumped from about two in a hundred to more than one in ten. Prices did fall, but the price was paid in jobs. Mattei argues that was part of the point: fewer jobs means workers can't ask for more. This is chapter 1's money part of austerity.
pages.sample_line: prices did fall... but the price was paid in jobs. mattei argues that was part of the point.
pages.on_screen: British high street 1920s (107). The bank object slides in and a big interest dial turns to 7% with a heavy thud on 'seven percent'. The iron weight drops onto the factory gate (109) and the chimney stops. The dole queue lengthens on 'more than one in ten'. On 'the money part of austerity' chapter 1's MONEY panel flips back up.

pages.name: Spent on what?
pages.what_is_said: In New Zealand the Reserve Bank pushed its rate from a quarter of a percent to five and a half, and unemployment climbed from 3.2% to 5.6%. Now it is raising rates again, against a rise that's mostly fuel. So when someone says creating money causes inflation, ask: spent on what? And who pays to stop it?
pages.sample_line: so when someone says creating money causes inflation... ask them. spent on what? and who pays to stop it?
pages.on_screen: Modern NZ street from page 7. The interest dial from page 9 turns from 0.25 to 5.5. The dole queue slides in on 'five point six'. The dial nudges up again on 'raising rates again' while the petrol pump stands beside it. Final beat: back in the parliament (101), the politician (201) faces the words SPENT ON WHAT? The page corner lifts.

draft.page_1_full_draft: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] So... won't creating money just cause inflation? It's the first thing people say, and it's a fair question. Inflation just means prices, in general, going up over time... usually measured over a year. Not one price tag. The whole shopping basket. To answer it, let's go back to where we started... the shell factory.
mattei_claims_marked_as_hers: Page 9: 'Mattei argues that was part of the point' (the 1920 interest-rate rise and the unemployment that followed), from C2-H17.

Page 9: 'Fewer jobs means workers can't ask for more', said straight after 'Mattei argues' as her reasoning, from C2-H18 (her The Nation and RevDem words on cooling the labour market and workers' bargaining power).
Page 9: 'Remember the money part of austerity?' points back to chapter 1's three parts, which chapter 1 already presented as Mattei's.
strengths: One concrete machine (the 1915 shell factory, split into an idle factory and a flat-out factory) carries the whole explanation, so 'it depends where the money is spent' becomes something the viewer can see.
It honestly admits the edge at once: the factory chapter 1 praised did see prices double, so the film can't be accused of hiding it.
It holds the user's hinge through every test: money with spare capacity (Japan, Britain), money with collapsing production (Germany, Zimbabwe), and costs with no new money (oil, NZ fuel).
It reuses chapter 1 heavily (about 30 reused paintings), so the paintings stay consistent and fal cost stays under a dollar.

It ends in New Zealand now (4.1% vs 2.9% without fuel, rates rising again, unemployment 5.6%), which suits a viewer weeks before the 7 November election, and it closes on a plain question the viewer can reuse: spent on what?
The plain names stay fixed throughout: 'creating money', 'price tag', 'flat out', 'shell factory'.
weaknesses_and_risks: Length: 591 words is near the top of the range. At 140 words a minute plus pauses it runs about 4 min 15 s, slightly over 4 minutes. Pages 3 and 9 (72-73 words, about 30 s each) are the first to trim. Dropping Zimbabwe or the Japan sentence saves about 15 s.

Page 2's 'more money chasing fewer goods' is the ledger's own simplification (C2-H03 is medium confidence, and the NBER detail was seen only in a summary). Which mattered more, shortages or credit, is open.

Page 3's two factories are a teaching model built on Keynes's 'true inflation' point (C2-M09). Prices can start rising before every machine is busy because of bottlenecks. The narration says the tag 'stays put', which is a simplification ('mostly stays put' would be safer).

Page 4: 'Some things can't be made more of in a hurry at all' is the film's general point. The ledger has no source saying Glasgow housing was short or that no homes were being built in 1915. 'Scarce food was shared, not bid up' is also the film's explanation, not a source quote (C2-H05 is medium confidence, from search summaries).

Page 5: 'the new money went into things people own' simplifies C2-C10, which says the Bank's purchases raised asset prices; it does not say the money literally went there. Britain's £895bn was built up from 2009 to 2020 and the 2015 zero came from falling fuel and food prices (C2-C08 caveat), so the narration says 'hundreds of billions' and does not claim a direct cause. A sharp viewer may still read it as one. Japan's 0.5% includes a 2014 tax rise, and mainstream economists credit weak demand and ageing, not just 'money sat idle'.

Page 5 avoids saying created money raised house prices, because the ledger could not verify a QE-to-house-price link. Page 8's NZ house price jump is linked only to the 'support' through the Royal Commission's 'in part' (C2-M10, C2-N14) and the review (C2-N15), and the review covered the Reserve Bank, not house prices directly.

Page 6: who caused what in Germany and Zimbabwe is disputed (reparations vs domestic deficits; supply collapse vs money first). The Zimbabwe output figures are secondary. 'Farms and factories collapsed first' takes one side of a live debate (C2-C04/C05 caveats). Hyperinflation footage risks being read as 'see, printing money does cause it'; the narration counts on 'coal and steel stop' to carry the point.

Page 7: the Fed's own history says the 1970s inflation started before the oil shock and blames loose policy too (C2-C14 caveat). The narration presents oil as a trigger for cost rises, not the whole story, but it does not say so out loud.

Page 9: whether the 1920 Bank Rate rise caused the slump, or only deepened a downturn already coming, is debated (C2-H08). The narration says 'within a year', which shows the order of events but does not claim cause. Mattei's 'part of the point' is contested (Glasner's criticism in C2-H17), and it is clearly marked as hers.

Page 10: 'a rise that's mostly fuel' is the film's framing from 4.1% vs 2.9% (C2-M18 caveat). The Reserve Bank cites broader worries such as core inflation and expectations. With an election on 7 November, this line may sound partisan; consider 'a rise driven largely by fuel' and keep the tone neutral. The July 2026 rate level is inferred, so the narration avoids naming it.
The ledger has no fact that New Zealand had idle workers or spare capacity at any point, so the 'idle factory' half of the rule is shown only with Japan and Britain, not with a New Zealand case.

Lerner, Kelton and Weber's alternative tools against inflation (taxes, targeted spending, buffer stocks) are left out to save time. The chapter shows the official cure's cost but offers no other cure, which a viewer may notice.

There are two new backgrounds in modern style (Tokyo shop, NZ street) beside 1920s ones. Keeping the painting style consistent across a 1915-to-2026 time jump needs care. The 100-trillion note and the yen notes must not copy real banknote designs closely.

pages.name: The question
pages.what_is_said: Picks up chapter 1's last question and calls it fair. Starts from the checkout: the same basket of shopping costs more than last year. That is inflation: prices in general going up over time, the whole basket and not one price tag. Then it heads back to the war and the shell factory.
pages.sample_line: that's inflation... prices in general going up over time. not one price tag... the whole basket.
pages.on_screen: Parliament (101) with the politician (201) and INFLATION? still standing from chapter 1's last frame. On 'the checkout' the shopping basket slides in. On 'not one price tag' a single blank price tag flips up. On 'the whole basket' the tag drops onto the basket. The page peels on 'the shell factory'.

pages.name: Back to the shell factory
pages.what_is_said: Britain, 1915: fewer than one in a hundred people are out of work. The war is paid for partly with new money, created through the banks. Submarines are sinking ships full of food and materials. So more money is chasing fewer things to buy, and by the end of the war prices have roughly doubled.
pages.sample_line: so more money is chasing fewer things to buy. by the end of the war... prices have roughly doubled.
pages.on_screen: Munitions factory (102) with the munition women (203) and the row of shells (209). On 'fewer than one in a hundred' the words UNDER 1 IN 100 OUT OF WORK pop up. On 'new money' a bundle of banknotes drops onto the money sack. On 'sinking ships' a small cargo-ship cut-out tips and slides down out of frame. On 'roughly doubled' the price tag from page 1 slides up to twice its height.

pages.name: Two factories
pages.what_is_said: The hinge. In a factory where machines stand idle, new money starts them and more shells come out, so the price tag mostly stays put. In a factory already running flat out, the same money can't make more shells, so buyers bid against each other and the price tag climbs. Britain in 1915 was the second factory.
pages.sample_line: the same money arrives... but no more shells can be made. so buyers bid against each other... and the price tag climbs.
pages.on_screen: The page splits into two copies of the small factory side by side. The left one is darkened, with the queue of workers (206) at its gate. The right one is lit, with a paper smoke puff above its chimney. Left: on 'new money arrives' coins drop in, the factory lightens, a smoke puff pops up, the workers slide in through the gate, and shells stack up beside a price tag that does not move. Right: coins drop in, no shells appear, and the price tag slides upward with a paper creak.

pages.name: Things you can't make more of in a hurry
pages.what_is_said: Some things can't be made more of in a hurry, like homes. In 1915 Glasgow landlords tried to push rents up by a quarter. About twenty thousand households refused to pay, and that November Parliament froze rents.
pages.sample_line: in 1915, glasgow landlords tried to push rents up by a quarter. about twenty thousand households refused to pay.
pages.on_screen: New background: a Glasgow tenement close. On 'by a quarter' a landlord's notice stamped +25% slaps onto the close. On 'refused to pay' the red banner unrolls across the windows. On 'froze rents' chapter 1's rubber stamp crashes down in dust and the +25% notice tears away.

pages.name: Test one: lots of new money, flat prices
pages.what_is_said: Test the rule. In 2013 Japan's central bank, which issues the yen, set out to double the money it had created within two years. Prices barely moved, about half a percent a year. Britain's central bank created hundreds of billions of pounds. Its own study found the new money pushed up the prices of things people own, like shares, and that the richest households gained most.
pages.sample_line: its own study found the new money pushed up the prices of things people own, like shares... and the richest households gained most.
pages.on_screen: New background: a Tokyo noodle-shop counter. A paper stack of yen notes grows taller in steps while the price tag on a bowl of noodles stays still. The page peels to the bank object. Banknotes slide out past the shopping basket, whose tag stays unchanged, and pile up beside a small share-price board, whose cut-out arrow slides up.
new_paintings: stack of yen notes, invented design (small object)

pages.name: Test two: when less is being made
pages.what_is_said: Germany, 1923. Prices are already rising fast. Then French and Belgian soldiers march into the Ruhr, Germany's coal and steel heartland. Workers down tools and the government keeps paying them with new money. By November one US dollar costs more than four trillion marks. This time new money really did push prices up, while less and less was being made.
pages.sample_line: workers down tools... and the government keeps paying them with new money. by november, one us dollar costs more than four trillion marks.
pages.on_screen: Pithead background with the soldiers sliding in from the side on 'soldiers march'. On 'down tools' the padlock clamps onto the pit gate and the pithead dims. On 'new money' notes pour into a wheelbarrow. On 'four trillion' a huge mark note, in an invented design, rises up the page.
new_paintings: huge mark note, invented design (small object)

pages.name: Test three: costs, not spending
pages.what_is_said: Sometimes the cause is costs, not spending. In 1973, with prices already climbing, the price of oil nearly quadrupled in three months, and everything made or moved with fuel got dearer. Here, prices rose 4.1% in the year to June. Take fuel out and it's 2.9%, inside the Reserve Bank's target.
pages.sample_line: here, prices rose four point one percent in the year to june. take fuel out... and it's two point nine.
pages.on_screen: An oil barrel crashes in with dust on '1973'. Its price tag flips from 2.90 to 11.65, and on 'got dearer' a row of price tags behind it tips up like dominoes. The page peels to a modern New Zealand street with a petrol pump. On 'take fuel out' the pump folds flat and the 4.1% tag flips over to 2.9%.

pages.name: The honest edge
pages.what_is_said: So yes, creating money can push prices up when it's spent where workers are already flat out, or on things we can't make more of in a hurry. In 2021 our unemployment fell to a record low and house prices jumped about thirty percent in a year. An independent review says the pandemic support was right at first, but too strong for too long.
pages.sample_line: so yes... creating money can push prices up, when it's spent where workers are already flat out, or on things we can't make more of in a hurry.
pages.on_screen: The right-hand, flat-out factory from page 3 comes back for one beat on 'flat out'. On 'in a hurry' a small New Zealand house pops up from flat. On 'thirty percent' the house rises on its pop-up and its price tag jumps. On 'independent review' the report object drops in with a typed card INDEPENDENT REVIEW 2026, and chapter 1's rubber stamp crashes onto it on 'too strong for too long'.
reused_paintings: royal commission report (relabelled with typed card)

pages.name: Who pays to fight it
pages.what_is_said: The usual cure: in April 1920 the Bank of England pushed its interest rate up to seven percent, so loans are dearer, people spend less and prices come down. Within a year unemployment jumped from about two in a hundred to more than one in ten. Prices did fall, but people paid with their jobs. Mattei argues that was part of the point of austerity's money part: with fewer jobs, workers can't ask for more.
pages.sample_line: prices did fall... but people paid with their jobs. mattei argues that was part of the point.
pages.on_screen: British high street 1920s (107). The bank object slides in, and on 'seven percent' the paper needle of an interest-rate dial swings to 7% with a heavy thud. The iron weight drops onto the factory gate (109) with dust and its windows dim. On 'more than one in ten' the dole queue slides in longer. On 'mattei argues' a typed name card CLARA E. MATTEI appears. On 'the money part' chapter 1's MONEY panel flips back up.
new_paintings: interest-rate dial with paper needle (small object)

pages.name: Spent on what?
pages.what_is_said: In New Zealand the Reserve Bank pushed its interest rate from a quarter of a percent to five and a half, and unemployment has climbed from 3.2% to 5.6%. Now it is raising its interest rate again. So when someone says creating money causes inflation, ask: spent on what? And who pays to stop it?
pages.sample_line: so when someone says creating money causes inflation... ask: spent on what? and who pays to stop it?
pages.on_screen: Modern New Zealand street from page 7. The dial from page 9 swings from 0.25 to 5.5. On 'five point six' the dole queue slides in. On 'raising its interest rate again' the needle nudges up a notch. Final beat: back in parliament (101), the politician (201) faces the words SPENT ON WHAT?, which replace INFLATION? from page 1. The page corner lifts.

revised.page_1_full_draft: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] so... won't creating money just cause inflation? it's a fair question. you've felt it at the checkout... the same basket of shopping costs more than last year. that's inflation... prices in general going up over time. not one price tag... the whole basket. so let's go back to the war... and the shell factory.
mattei_claims_marked_as_hers: Page 9: 'mattei argues that was part of the point' (that the unemployment after the 1920 interest-rate rise was intended), from C2-H17. It is said after the official reason (dearer loans, less spending, lower prices, from C2-M17), so the two views are kept apart.

Page 9: 'the money part of austerity. fewer jobs, and workers can't ask for more' is said in the same sentence as 'mattei argues', as her reasoning, from C2-H18 (The Nation and RevDem 2023: rate rises cool the labour market and lower workers' bargaining power). The MONEY panel points back to chapter 1's three parts, which chapter 1 presented as Mattei's.
strengths: One concrete machine, chapter 1's 1915 shell factory split into an idle factory and a flat-out factory, carries the whole explanation. That turns the user's point ('it depends where and how the money is spent') into something the viewer can see.

The honest edge comes early and plainly (page 2: prices doubled in the factory chapter 1 praised) and again on pages 6 and 8. Page 9 states the official reason for raising interest rates before Mattei's reading, so the film is fair to both sides.

Each test case lines up with the rule: idle money with spare capacity (Japan, and Britain's money going into shares), money poured in while less is made (Germany 1923), and costs rather than spending (oil in 1973, New Zealand fuel now).
Page 8 now has a New Zealand flat-out case: record-low unemployment in 2021 alongside the house-price jump. Page 10's '3.2% to 5.6%' pays it off.
It reuses chapter 1 heavily (about 30 reused paintings) and needs only 3 new backgrounds and 11 small objects, so fal cost stays well under budget.
The plain names stay fixed throughout: 'new money', 'creating money', 'price tag', 'flat out', 'interest rate', 'the basket', 'things'.
weaknesses_and_risks: Changed: page 10 previously said the Reserve Bank was raising rates 'against a rise that's mostly fuel'. That is wrong arithmetic: fuel adds about 1.2 points of the 4.1%, and 2.9% is still non-fuel inflation (C2-N05, C2-M18 caveat). The line was cut. Page 7 now says the plainer fact: without fuel, inflation is 2.9%, inside the Reserve Bank's target. This also keeps page 10 neutral before the 7 November election.

Changed: page 8 previously put the words 'too strong for too long' on the royal commission report. That phrase comes from the independent review (C2-N15), not the Royal Commission (C2-N14). The narration and the typed card now name the independent review, and C2-N14 was removed from that page's ids.

Changed: page 8 listed C2-N09 (unemployment at 3.2%) as a source but never said it. It is now said ('our unemployment fell to a record low'), which gives New Zealand its own flat-out case and fixes the old open point that only Japan and Britain showed the rule.

Changed: page 8 previously said 'things we can't make more of, like land, houses and oil'. Oil can be made more of over time, and page 7 already treats oil as a cost shock, so oil was cut. The wording is now 'can't make more of in a hurry', the same phrase as page 4's homes.

Changed: page 5's Britain line previously implied that huge money creation left 2015 prices at zero. The ledger says the 2015 zero came from fuel and food prices, and the £895bn was built up over 2009-2020, including about £450bn in 2020 that was followed by inflation (C2-C08). The 2015 claim and the '2015: 0%' card were dropped. Britain now shows only where the new money went (C2-C10). The 2012 study's finding is said as 'pushed up the prices of things people own, like shares' (not 'the money went into'). 'Gains went mostly to the wealthiest' became 'the richest households gained most', because the source says the top 5% held 40%, not most.

Changed: page 6 previously said coal and steel 'stopped'. The ledger has no figure and says only that output fell, so this became 'while less and less was being made'. Added 'prices are already rising fast', because the Ruhr turned high inflation into hyperinflation and did not start it (C2-C02 caveat). The soldiers are named as French and Belgian.

Changed: Zimbabwe was cut from page 6. Its output figures are second-hand (C2-C04 is medium confidence, and the IMF 40%/14% figures are in could_not_verify), and 'farms collapsed first, then the money' takes one side of a live debate. This also saves about 15 seconds and one painting.

Changed: page 7 now adds 'with prices already climbing' before the 1973 oil shock, because the Fed's own history says the Great Inflation began before it (C2-C14 caveat). The pitch no longer says 'no new money involved'. The screen card became '1973: OIL NEARLY x4' to match 'nearly quadrupled'.

Changed: rationing (C2-H05) was cut from page 4. It was medium confidence from search summaries, and its 'shared, not bid up' line was the film's own explanation. Cutting it also saves about 20 seconds and two small paintings (ration book, sugar bag). Page 4 now ends on 'that november, parliament froze rents', which matches the dates (strike by November 1915, Act passed 27 November) better than 'within weeks'.

Changed: page 9's 'prices did fall... but the price was paid in jobs' used 'price' for two things. It is now 'people paid with their jobs'. Added the official mechanism ('dearer loans, less spending, lower prices', C2-M17) before Mattei, so her reading is clearly one view.

Changed: page_1_full_draft used capitals, which breaks the rules. It is now all lower case apart from the required accent tag. A concrete case now comes before the definition ('you've felt it at the checkout... the same basket of shopping costs more than last year'). 'Usually measured over a year' was cut as a repeat of 'than last year'.

Changed: page 3's 'the price tag stays put' became 'mostly stays put', because prices can rise before every machine is busy (Keynes, C2-M09). 'Workers wait at the gate' was cut from the narration because the picture shows it.

Changed: synonyms removed to keep one plain name per thing. 'Newly created money' and 'created money' became 'new money'. 'Goods' became 'things'. 'Workers who are already busy' became 'flat out'. Bare 'rate' became 'interest rate'. 'Shares and bonds' became 'shares', so 'bonds' did not need explaining. 'Central bank' is explained at first use ('which issues the yen').

Changed: on-screen movement was made paper-only. The pit wheel 'stopping' and chimneys 'going cold' were not possible with still paintings. They became a padlock clamping on and the painting dimming, a paper smoke-puff cut-out, and a dial with a separate paper needle. Banknotes are invented designs, not copies of real notes. Mattei appears only as a typed name card.

Changed: the painting count went from 4 large and 14 small to 3 large and 11 small. The pithead is reused for the Ruhr, and the ration book, sugar bag, dry field and Zimbabwe notes were cut. The smoke puff, a share board with arrow and an invented mark note were added or kept. The fal estimate rose from $0.75 to about $1.75, which allows roughly three attempts per painting for style matching (3 x $0.10 + 11 x $0.025 = $0.58 per pass).

Still open: the length is 582 words, about 4 min 8 s at chapter 1's pace (520 words in 3:41), slightly over 4 minutes. If it must come in under 4:00, cut first 'with prices already climbing' (page 7) and 'which issues the yen' (page 5), or shorten page 9's official-mechanism line.

Still open: page 2's 'more money is chasing fewer things to buy' and 'britain in 1915 was the second factory' (page 3) are the film's simplification. C2-H03 is medium confidence, and its NBER detail was seen only in a summary. Whether shortages or credit mattered more is open.
Still open: page 4's 'some things can't be made more of in a hurry... like homes' is the film's general point. No ledger entry says Glasgow housing was short in 1915.

Still open: page 8 places record-low unemployment, the house-price jump and the review's verdict side by side, which suggests a cause. The Royal Commission says the response raised house prices only 'in part', with international forces too (C2-M10, C2-N14). House prices are not in the CPI. Low interest rates and housing shortages also played a part (C2-N08). Consider adding 'in part' if there is time.

Still open: page 9's link from the 1920 rate rise to the slump is debated (C2-H08). The narration only gives the order of events ('within a year'), but viewers may read it as cause. Glasner disputes Mattei's 'part of the point' reading (C2-H17).

Still open: page 10 sets the rise in unemployment from 3.2% to 5.6% next to the rate rises. That direction is the mainstream account (C2-N11), but the 2023 recessions also involved cyclones, and 5.6% came after rates were already being cut. The line states only the figures.

Still open: the film shows the cost of the official cure but gives no alternative cure, because Lerner's and Weber's tools (taxes, buffer stocks) were left out to save time. Viewers may ask 'so what instead?', which could open chapter 3.

Still open: the three new backgrounds (Glasgow 1915, Tokyo, modern New Zealand) span a hundred years. Keeping one painted-paper style across them needs reference images taken from chapter 1's paintings.

draft.title: What happened next
draft.angle: B - the story continues, 1919 to today
draft.pitch: You go back to the shell factory and watch what happened to prices: they really did double, because the war's spending chased workers, ships and food that had run out. Then you see the experts' cure in action: a 7% interest rate, a slump, council homes cut, gold and the miners. Then "sound familiar?" lands you in New Zealand 2020-2026, where new money chased houses, the same cure came back, and you come away knowing it's not whether money is created but what it buys, and whether more of that thing can be made.
draft.the_one_idea: Creating money pushes prices up when the spending chases things that have run out or can't quickly be made, like workers in 1918 or houses in 2021, so what matters is where and how it is spent.
draft.how_it_explains_inflation_through_chapte: It picks up the same story at the same places. Page 2 is chapter 1's shell factory and its line "it can run out of workers, materials and machines". This time the viewer sees that this is exactly when prices rise: almost everyone had a job, ships were being sunk, and new money and bank credit were chasing what was left. The Glasgow square becomes the Glasgow rent strike. The pay packet and price tag from chapter 1 page 2 carry the numbers. The experts' five cards (stop creating new money, rates to banks, back to gold) come back as the cure that actually got used: the iron weight drops as the 7% rate, the council houses fold away, gold crashes onto the pay packet, and the miner with the paper jaw from page 3 returns for 1926. Chapter 1's politician returns for "sound familiar?" in 2020s New Zealand, and the cure (iron weight, dole queue) is reused there. The closing rule turns chapter 1's "it can run out of workers, materials and machines" into the test for inflation.
draft.honest_edge: It is said plainly on page 2, from inside the story rather than as a lecture: yes, in the war new money did push prices up, because it was chasing workers, ships and food that had run out (C2-H01, C2-H02, C2-H03). It comes back on page 8: in 2021 a lot of the new money ended up in houses, which can't quickly be built, and the Royal Commission found the pandemic response helped push house prices up, in part (C2-N08, C2-N14, C2-M10). The independent review's "too strong for too long" is quoted too (C2-N15). On page 10 the rule is stated with both sides: new money that chases things that have run out turns into higher prices, and where there are idle workers it "mostly" gets them working (C2-M09, said with "mostly", not "never").

pages.name: The price tag
pages.what_is_said: Picks up chapter 1's question, defines inflation in plain words, then shows it really happened in chapter 1's own story: British prices doubled in the war and were about two and a half times higher by 1920. Was it the new money? Back to the shell factory.
pages.sample_line: by 1920 they were about two and a half times what they'd been in 1914... so was it the new money?
pages.on_screen: Chapter 1's last frame (the politician in the parliament, money stack, price tag, INFLATION?) holds, then the page peels. A blank price tag and a shopping basket flip up on 'prices, in general, going up'. On 'roughly doubled' the price tag swells with a paper crinkle; on 'two and a half times' it swells again. The 1915 shell factory slides in behind on 'back to the shell factory'.

pages.name: What ran out
pages.what_is_said: The war was paid for partly with new money and bank credit. But almost everyone who could work already had a job, and submarines sank millions of tons of shipping. So the new money was chasing workers, ships and food that had run out, and that is when prices rise. The honest edge, said straight.
pages.sample_line: remember... a country can run out of workers, materials and machines. in the war, it did. and that's when the new money turned into higher prices.
pages.on_screen: Munition women and shells in the 1915 factory. A bundle of banknotes drops in on 'new money'. On 'almost everyone had a job' the queue of workers slides in and folds into the factory until the gate is empty. A cargo ship slides across and sinks below a paper sea on 'submarines'. On 'chasing' the banknotes slide toward a shrinking pile of goods and the price tag pops higher.

pages.name: Rent and sugar
pages.what_is_said: Where it hurt and how people pushed back: Glasgow landlords tried a 25% rent rise in 1915, about twenty thousand households refused to pay, and Parliament froze rents within weeks. By 1918 the government was buying most food and rationing sugar, meat and butter, so scarce food was shared rather than going to whoever could pay most.
pages.sample_line: about twenty thousand households refused to pay... and within weeks, Parliament froze rents.
pages.on_screen: A Glasgow tenement close with women at the windows. A landlord's notice stamped +25% slaps onto the door, then tears away on 'refused to pay'. The royal commission report style scroll crashes down as a law on 'froze rents'. Page peels to the 1920 kitchen: a ration book and a half-pound bag of sugar flip up on 'rationing'.
new_paintings: Glasgow tenement close with women at windows (background)

pages.name: The boom and the cure
pages.what_is_said: The war ends, businesses rush to rebuild and restock, and prices climb about 15% more in 1920. Then the experts' cure: in April 1920 the Bank of England pushes its interest rate (the price of borrowing) up to 7% and holds it for about a year. Borrowing is made expensive on purpose.
pages.sample_line: in April 1920 the Bank of England pushed its interest rate... the price of borrowing... up to seven percent. and held it there for about a year.
pages.on_screen: The 1920s high street, busy; shipyard-style scaffolding and stacks of building materials pop up on 'rebuild and restock'; the price tag pops again on 'fifteen percent'. Chapter 1's bankers' table slides in. On 'seven percent' the iron weight crashes onto the street with dust and a dial reading 7% flips up.
new_paintings: interest-rate dial (small, numbers added in edit so it can be reused for New Zealand)

pages.name: The slump
pages.what_is_said: Within a year unemployment jumps from about two in a hundred to more than one in ten, and everything the country makes falls by around a fifth. Prices do fall, by about a fifth in two years. But the price was paid in jobs, and of half a million promised council homes only about two hundred thousand were built when the cuts came.
pages.sample_line: and prices did fall... by about a fifth in two years. but the price was paid in jobs.
pages.on_screen: The factory gate 1920s: the chimney stops smoking and the dole queue slides in, growing on 'more than one in ten'. A bar jumps from 2 to 11. The price tag shrinks on 'prices did fall'. Council houses flip up in a row, then most fold flat on 'when the cuts came', leaving half-built frames with scaffolding.

pages.name: Who was it for?
pages.what_is_said: Mattei argues the 1920 rate jump wasn't just about prices: it made lenders' money worth more again and threw people out of work, and she says that was part of the point. In her reading, fewer jobs means workers can't ask for more, so unemployment becomes a way to keep wages down.
pages.sample_line: Mattei argues the rate jump wasn't just about prices... it made lenders' money worth more again. and she says putting people out of work was part of the point.
pages.on_screen: The boardroom 1920: the three industrialists in top hats and a money sack. On 'lenders' money worth more' the money sack swells. A typed name card 'Clara E. Mattei, The Capital Order' and the red book flip up. On 'keep wages down' the pay packet is squashed under the iron weight, and the dole queue from page 5 slides in at the bottom edge.

pages.name: Gold and the miners
pages.what_is_said: In 1925 Britain went back on gold at the old pre-war rate. Even today's Bank of England governor says the pound was set too high, so wages and prices had to be forced down to fit. The coal owners demanded lower pay and longer hours; in 1926 about one and a half million walked out for nine days; the miners held out for months, and lost.
pages.sample_line: even today's Bank of England governor says the pound was set too high... so wages and prices had to be forced down to fit.
pages.on_screen: Gold bars crash onto a balance scale; a pound note sits on the other pan and a pay packet slides off on 'forced down'. Typed name card for the governor's 2025 speech (no portrait). Page peels to the pithead: the miner with the paper jaw from chapter 1 returns; a crowd flips up on 'walked out'; on 'and lost' the crowd folds down one row at a time.

pages.name: Sound familiar?
pages.what_is_said: Jump to New Zealand, 2020. The Reserve Bank created new money to buy about fifty-three billion dollars of government bonds (government IOUs) and lent banks about nineteen billion, cheap. Where did it go? A lot of it into houses: prices jumped about thirty percent in a year in 2021, and a Royal Commission found the pandemic response helped push them up, in part. You can't quickly make more land. By mid-2022 prices overall were rising 7.3% a year, petrol up a third and building a new house up nearly a fifth.
pages.sample_line: where did the new money go? a lot of it went into houses... and you can't quickly make more land.
pages.on_screen: Chapter 1's politician returns with his paper jaw on 'sound familiar?', then the page peels to a 2021 New Zealand suburban street. The bank object prints a ribbon of banknotes onto a bond IOU marked 53 BILLION. A house pops up and a price tag on it swells on 'thirty percent'. The farmland plot stays the same size while money sacks pile on, on 'more land'. A petrol pump and a timber house frame flip up on 'petrol' and 'building a new house'.

pages.name: The cure, again
pages.what_is_said: Then the same cure: the Reserve Bank pushed its interest rate from a quarter of a percent up to five and a half in under two years. The economy shrank, twice, and unemployment climbed from 3.2% to 5.6%. An independent review now says the support was right at first but 'too strong for too long'. Mattei sees the same pattern today in Europe and America: when prices rise and workers start asking for more, the old cure comes back.
pages.sample_line: same cure... a quarter of a percent, up to five and a half. the economy shrank, twice. and unemployment climbed from three point two to five point six.
pages.on_screen: Back to the New Zealand street. The interest-rate dial from page 4 spins from 0.25 to 5.5; on 'five and a half' the iron weight crashes down with dust. A small factory's chimney stops and the dole queue slides in, growing on 'five point six'. The royal commission report object returns as the review and the rubber stamp slaps TOO STRONG FOR TOO LONG on it. The red book and 'Mattei argues' card flip up briefly on the last line.

pages.name: What it buys
pages.what_is_said: So does creating money cause inflation? It depends what it buys. In 1918 it chased workers and ships that had run out; in 2021 a lot of it chased houses. Where there are idle workers and empty factories, new spending mostly gets them working. The limit isn't money, it's workers, materials and machines. And today: prices up 4.1%, 2.9% without fuel, and the Reserve Bank is raising rates again, with unemployment at a ten-year high. Nobody has yet split how much of the 2021-23 rise came from here and how much from the world.
pages.sample_line: so it's not whether money is created... it's what it buys. and whether there's room to make more of it.
pages.on_screen: Two small factories side by side. On the left, idle workers; coins drop in and the machines start and goods pop up (no price change). On the right, a factory already full; coins drop in and only the price tag rises. On 'workers, materials and machines' the three flip up exactly as in chapter 1 page 8. Back to the parliament: the politician stands; the price tag reads 4.1%, then the fuel pump folds away and it reads 2.9%. The iron weight hovers above on 'raising rates again'. The page corner lifts.

draft.page_1_full_draft: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] So... won't creating money just cause inflation? First, the word. Inflation means prices, in general, going up over time... usually measured over a year. And in the story from last time, they did go up. In Britain, everyday prices roughly doubled during the war. By 1920, they were about two and a half times what they'd been in 1914. So was it the new money? Let's go back to the shell factory.

Page 6: putting people out of work was part of the point (C2-H17), said as 'she says'.
Page 6: fewer jobs means workers can't ask for more, so unemployment becomes a way to keep wages down (C2-H18), said as 'in her reading' / 'Mattei argues'.

Page 9: the same pattern today in Europe and America; when prices rise and workers start asking for more, the old cure comes back (C2-H19), said as 'Mattei sees the same pattern'. She was not talking about New Zealand, and the narration must not say she was.
strengths: It is chapter 1 carried on: the same factory, Glasgow, kitchen, pithead, miner, bankers, iron weight, dole queue and politician. So inflation is explained inside the world the viewer already knows, and most paintings are reused (about 40 reused, 18 new).

The honest edge comes out of the story, not a lecture. On page 2 the viewer sees chapter 1's own line ('it can run out of workers, materials and machines') turn into the reason prices rose, with low unemployment and sunk ships as the concrete case.
The user's hinge (where and how money is spent) is shown twice with real cases a century apart, 1918 (workers, ships) and 2021 (houses), before it is stated as a rule on page 10.
It pays off chapter 1's experts' advice: the viewer sees what 'stop creating new money, rates to central banks, back to gold' did to jobs, council homes and miners.
'Sound familiar?' echoes chapter 1's ending and makes the New Zealand part hit home a month before the election, using only actual released figures (7.3%, 5.5%, 3.2% to 5.6%, 4.1%/2.9%).
Cheap: about 75 US cents of new paintings, leaving lots of room for re-paints inside the US$10 limit.
weaknesses_and_risks: Too many numbers. Every page has two or three figures (x2, x2.5, 15%, 7%, 2 to 11 in 100, a fifth, 500,000/213,000, 53 billion, 30%, 7.3%, 0.25 to 5.5, 3.2 to 5.6, 4.1/2.9). A listener may lose the one idea. The on-screen words should carry the numbers, and some may need cutting in the script pass.

Word count is tight. 570 words is near the 600 top, and page 8 (about 85 words) and page 10 (about 80) are over the 30-second page limit as sketched. Page 8 may need splitting or trimming (drop the bonds IOU or the FLP nineteen billion).

The explanation of what inflation is gets less teaching time than in a mechanism-first angle. Cost-push (fuel), expectations and profits are only touched on, through petrol in 2022 and 2026. The viewer learns 'what it buys' but not the full list of causes.

Weight of causes in 1914-1920 is contested (C2-H03 is medium confidence, the NBER detail was seen only in a search summary). 'More money, fewer goods' is a simplification, and the narration must not claim shortages, not money, were the whole cause. As written, both are given a part.

The ledger has no figure for how far wages were cut in 1920-22 ('wages pushed down' in the angle brief is unverified). The draft relies on Bailey's 2025 statement (C2-H12) that wages and prices had to be forced down after 1925, and the Samuel Commission's 13.5% recommendation (C2-H13), which is a recommendation, not the actual cut. No general 1920s wage-fall number can be said.

Whether the 7% rate caused the 1920-21 slump or only deepened a boom already collapsing is debated (C2-H08). The narration says 'then came the crash' after the rate rise, which suggests a cause. It may need 'and then' wording or a short 'historians still argue how much' line.
Council homes: the end date differs by source (June 1921 vs 1922), and linking the cut to the Geddes Axe is a simplification (C2-H10, C2-H11). The draft says 'when the cuts came' to stay safe.

Houses are not in the CPI (C2-N08, C2-M10). The film must not imply that house prices made up the 7.3%. The draft keeps them separate ('a lot of it went into houses' vs 'prices overall... petrol, building a new house'), but viewers may still merge them. 'You can't quickly make more land' is the film's own point, not the Royal Commission's.

No published estimate splits NZ's 2021-23 inflation between government spending, the Reserve Bank and world prices (C2-N16). The NZ case therefore shows the honest edge (houses), but can't prove how much of the 7.3% came from the new money. The draft says so on page 10, which costs words.

Linking Reserve Bank money creation to house prices: no quantified RBNZ or Treasury estimate exists (could_not_verify). The Royal Commission's 'in part' is about the whole economic response, so the narration must say 'helped push up, in part' and not 'the new money caused'.
'Tens of thousands more out of work' is not sourced; use the percentages only.

Election neutrality (7 November 2026). Page 9-10's 'the cure, again' and 'raising rates again' with a ten-year-high jobless rate could read as partisan. The independent review was commissioned by the current government and its timing was questioned (C2-N15). Keep to released figures, with no party names. 'Mostly fuel' is the film's framing from 4.1 vs 2.9 (C2-M18); the Bank cites wider concerns.

Mattei's 'same pattern today' (C2-H19) was about the US and Europe in 2022-23, not New Zealand. Placing it on the NZ page risks implying she said it about NZ, so it must be worded 'in Europe and America'.

The two halves (1914-1926 and 2020-2026) leave a 94-year jump. Without the politician and 'sound familiar?' bridge, it may feel like two films. Chapter 1 also already used 'sound familiar?', so the echo may feel repeated.
Some period images need checking: the 1926 'not a penny off the pay' banner is unconfirmed (not used here), and the tram and tenement pictures must not show real people or wrong-era details.

The Bank of England governor appears only as a typed name card. His 2025 view is quoted to show even the mainstream agrees on the 1925 pound. Some viewers may take that as the Bank endorsing Mattei; it does not.

revised.title: What happened next
revised.angle: B - the story continues, 1919 to today
revised.pitch: You go back to chapter 1's shell factory and see prices really did double, because the war's new money was chasing workers, ships and food that had run out. Then you watch the cure at work: a 7% interest rate, a slump, council homes cut, gold and the miners. Then "sound familiar?" brings you to New Zealand from 2020 to 2026, where house prices and building costs ran hot and the same kind of cure came back. You come away knowing that new money doesn't cause inflation in itself. It depends where and how it's spent.
revised.the_one_idea: New money pushes prices up when it is spent chasing things that have run out or can't quickly be made, like workers in 1918 or houses in 2021, so what matters is where and how it is spent.
revised.how_it_explains_inflation_through_chapte: It picks up the story in chapter 1's own places. Page 1 answers chapter 1's last question word for word. Page 2 goes back to the 1915 shell factory and turns chapter 1's line "it can run out of workers, materials and machines" into the reason prices rose: almost everyone had a job, ships were being sunk, and the new money paying for the war was chasing what was left. The pay packet, price tag and kitchen come back to carry the numbers. Chapter 1's experts advised making borrowing expensive and going back on gold, and here the viewer sees that cure used. The iron weight drops as the 7% interest rate, the council houses fold away, gold tips the scale against the pay packet, and the pithead and the miner with the paper jaw return for 1926. Chapter 1's politician comes back for "sound familiar?" to bring us to New Zealand, where the iron weight and dole queue are used again. The closing rule repeats chapter 1's "workers, materials and machines" as the test for inflation.
revised.honest_edge: It is said plainly on page 2, from inside the story: yes, in the war new money did push prices up, because it was chasing workers, ships and food that had run out (C2-H01, C2-H02, C2-H03). The narration also admits that historians still argue how much was money and how much was shortage. It comes back on page 8: house prices jumped about thirty percent in 2021, and a Royal Commission found the pandemic response helped push them up, in part (C2-N08, C2-N14, C2-M10). Page 9 quotes the independent review: support was right at first but "too strong for too long" (C2-N15). Page 10 gives the rule with both sides: when new money chases things that have run out, prices rise, and where workers and factories sit idle it "mostly" gets them working (C2-M09, said with "mostly", not "never"). Page 8 also says plainly that nobody has split New Zealand's inflation between home causes and the world (C2-N16).

pages.name: The price tag
pages.what_is_said: Answers chapter 1's last question. Gives inflation a plain meaning, then shows it really happened in chapter 1's story: British prices about doubled in the war and were about two and a half times higher by 1920. Was it the new money?
pages.sample_line: by 1920 they were about two and a half times what they'd been in 1914... so was it the new money?
pages.on_screen: Chapter 1's last frame holds: the parliament, the politician, the money stack, the price tag and INFLATION?. Then the page peels. On 'prices, in general, going up' a shopping basket pops up from flat with a blank price tag. On 'roughly doubled' the price tag pops up a size larger with a paper crinkle, and on 'two and a half times' it pops up larger again. On 'back to the shell factory' the 1915 munitions factory slides in behind.

pages.name: What ran out
pages.what_is_said: Chapter 1 said a country can run out of workers, materials and machines, and in the war Britain did. Fewer than one in a hundred were out of work, and submarines sank nearly eight million tons of shipping. The new money paying for the war was chasing what was left, so prices rose. Historians still argue how much was money and how much was shortage.
pages.sample_line: remember... a country can run out of workers, materials and machines. in the war, it did.
pages.on_screen: Munition women and shells in the 1915 factory. On 'out of work' the queue of workers slides into the factory gate until the gate is empty. On 'submarines' a cargo ship slides across a paper sea strip and sinks below it. On 'new money' a bundle of banknotes drops in and slides toward a small pile of goods, and the price tag pops up higher.

pages.name: Rent and sugar
pages.what_is_said: Where it hurt and how people pushed back. In 1915 Glasgow landlords tried a rent rise of a quarter, about twenty thousand households refused to pay, and within weeks Parliament froze rents. By 1918 the government controlled almost all food and rationed sugar, meat and butter, so scarce food was shared rather than bid up.
pages.sample_line: about twenty thousand households refused to pay... and within weeks, Parliament froze rents.
pages.on_screen: A Glasgow tenement close with women at the windows (painted, unnamed). A landlord's notice marked +25% slaps onto the door, then tears away on 'refused to pay'. On 'froze rents' the royal commission report crashes down as the new law, and the rubber stamp hits it. The page peels to the 1920 kitchen, where a ration book and a bag of sugar pop up on 'rationed'.
new_paintings: Glasgow tenement close with women at windows (background)

pages.name: The boom and the cure
pages.what_is_said: The war ends, businesses rush to rebuild and restock, and prices climb about fifteen percent more in 1920. Then comes the cure. In April 1920 the Bank of England pushes its interest rate, the price of borrowing, up to seven percent and holds it there for about a year.
pages.sample_line: in April 1920 the Bank of England pushes its interest rate... the price of borrowing... up to seven percent.
pages.on_screen: The 1920s high street, busy. Building materials pop up on 'rebuild and restock', and the price tag pops higher on 'fifteen percent'. Chapter 1's bankers' table slides in. On 'seven percent' the iron weight crashes onto the street with dust, and a paper dial reading 7% pops up beside it.
new_paintings: interest-rate dial (small, numbers added in the edit so it can be used again for New Zealand)

pages.name: The slump
pages.what_is_said: Within a year unemployment jumps from about two in a hundred to more than one in ten. How much the interest rate caused that is still argued. Prices do fall, by about a fifth in two years, but the price is paid in jobs. Of half a million promised council homes, only about two hundred thousand get built.
pages.sample_line: prices do fall... by about a fifth in two years. but the price is paid in jobs.
pages.on_screen: The 1920s factory gate. The chimney smoke slides away and the dole queue slides in, longer on 'more than one in ten'. A paper bar steps up from 2 to 1 in 10. The price tag shrinks on 'prices do fall'. A row of council houses pops up, then most fold flat on 'only about two hundred thousand', leaving half-built frames.

pages.name: Who was it for?
pages.what_is_said: Mattei argues the interest rate wasn't just about prices. It made lenders' money worth more again, and she says putting people out of work was part of the point: fewer jobs, and workers can't ask for more. Central banks see it differently: lost jobs are a cost, not the goal.
pages.sample_line: Mattei argues the interest rate wasn't just about prices... it made lenders' money worth more again.
pages.on_screen: The 1920 boardroom with the three industrialists in top hats. On 'lenders' money worth more' the money sack pops up larger. A typed name card 'Clara E. Mattei, The Capital Order' and the red book pop up. On 'workers can't ask for more' the iron weight drops onto the blank pay packet. On 'central banks see it differently' the bankers' table slides in at the bottom edge.

pages.name: Gold and the miners
pages.what_is_said: In 1925 Britain went back on gold at the old pre-war rate. Even today's Bank of England governor says the pound was set too high, so wages and prices had to be forced down. Coal owners wanted lower pay and longer hours; in 1926 about one and a half million workers walked out; the miners held out for months, and lost.
pages.sample_line: even today's Bank of England governor says the pound was set too high... so wages and prices had to be forced down.
pages.on_screen: Gold bars crash onto one pan of a balance scale. The pan with the pound note and pay packet tips, and the pay packet slides off on 'forced down'. A typed card 'Bank of England governor, 2025' appears (no portrait). The page peels to the pithead. The miner with the paper jaw returns, and the crowds pop up on 'walked out'. On 'and lost' they fold down one row at a time.

pages.name: Sound familiar?
pages.what_is_said: New Zealand, 2020. When covid hit, the Reserve Bank created about fifty-three billion dollars of new money to buy up government debt. House prices jumped about thirty percent in a year, and a Royal Commission found the pandemic response helped push them up, in part. You can't quickly make more land. By 2022 prices overall rose 7.3% in a year. How much of that came from here and how much from the world, nobody has split.
pages.sample_line: house prices jumped about thirty percent in a year... and you can't quickly make more land.
pages.on_screen: Chapter 1's politician returns, paper jaw moving, on 'sound familiar?'. The page peels to a 2021 New Zealand suburban street. The bank slides in with a bundle of banknotes and a 'government debt' certificate marked 53 BILLION. A house pops up, and on 'thirty percent' its price tag pops up larger. On 'more land' money sacks stack onto the farmland plot, which stays the same size. On 'seven point three' the blank price tag returns with the figure.

pages.name: The cure, again
pages.what_is_said: Then the same kind of cure. The Reserve Bank pushed its interest rate from a quarter of a percent to five and a half in under two years. The economy shrank twice, and unemployment has climbed from 3.2% to 5.6%. An independent review says the support was right at first but too strong for too long.
pages.sample_line: the Reserve Bank pushed its interest rate from a quarter of a percent to five and a half, in under two years.
pages.on_screen: The New Zealand street. Page 4's interest-rate dial turns in paper steps from 0.25 to 5.5, and on 'five and a half' the iron weight crashes down with dust. A small factory's chimney smoke slides away and the dole queue slides in, longer on 'five point six'. The royal commission report returns as the review, and the rubber stamp hits it with TOO STRONG FOR TOO LONG.

pages.name: Where and how it's spent
pages.what_is_said: So does new money cause inflation? It depends where and how it's spent. When it chases things that have run out, like workers in 1918, prices rise; where workers and factories sit idle, it mostly gets them working. Economists who study how modern money works say the limit isn't money, it's workers, materials and machines. And today: 4.1%, and 2.9% without fuel.
pages.sample_line: so does new money cause inflation? it depends where and how it's spent.
pages.on_screen: Two small factories side by side. On the left, the queue of workers waits outside an idle factory. Coins drop in, the workers slide inside, smoke slides out of the chimney and goods pop up, and the price tag stays still. On the right, a full factory: coins drop in and only the price tag pops up. On 'workers, materials and machines' the worker, the building materials and the lathe pop up as in chapter 1 page 8. Back in the parliament, the politician stands while the price tag reads 4.1%. A petrol pump folds away and the tag reads 2.9%. The page corner lifts.

revised.page_1_full_draft: [in a warm, steady New Zealand accent] So... won't creating money just cause inflation? Inflation means prices, in general, going up over time. And in last time's story, they did. In Britain, everyday prices roughly doubled during the war... and by 1920 they were about two and a half times what they'd been in 1914. So was it the new money? Back to the shell factory.
mattei_claims_marked_as_hers: Page 6: the 1920 interest rate wasn't just about prices; it made lenders' money worth more again (C2-H17). Said as 'Mattei argues'.
Page 6: putting people out of work was part of the point (C2-H17). Said as 'she says'.
Page 6: with fewer jobs, workers can't ask for more (C2-H18). Said in the same 'she says' sentence and followed at once by the central banks' view (C2-M17): 'lost jobs are a cost, not the goal'.
strengths: It is chapter 1 carried on. The same factory, kitchen, pithead, miner, bankers, iron weight, dole queue and politician return, so inflation is explained inside a world the viewer already knows. About 50 painting uses are reused, and 15 paintings are new.
The honest edge comes out of the story, not a lecture. Chapter 1's line 'it can run out of workers, materials and machines' becomes the reason prices rose in 1918.
The user's point, 'it depends where and how the money is spent', is shown with real cases a century apart (1918 workers and ships, 2021 houses). On page 10 it is then said in the user's own words.
It shows what chapter 1's advice did once it was used, in jobs, council homes and miners' pay.
Every New Zealand number is an actual released figure (7.3%, 0.25 to 5.5, 3.2 to 5.6, 4.1/2.9). The chapter names no party.
It is cheap: about 60 US cents of new paintings, or about US$1.75 allowing three tries each. That is well inside the US$10 limit.
weaknesses_and_risks: Changed: cut the Funding for Lending 'nineteen billion' line. Banks drew most of it in 2022, after interest rates were already rising (C2-N07), so putting it beside the 2021 house prices was misleading. It also saved words.

Changed: 'a lot of the new money went into houses' became two separate facts. House prices jumped about thirty percent (C2-N08), and the Royal Commission says the pandemic response helped push them up, 'in part' (C2-N14, C2-M10). No source measures how much Reserve Bank money went into houses (could_not_verify).

Changed: the Reserve Bank's purchases are now 'created new money to buy up government debt' instead of 'government bonds (IOUs)'. This drops an unexplained term. The bonds were bought from investors, not from the government directly (C2-N06).
Changed: 'then came the crash' after the 7% rate implied it caused the slump. Page 5 now says 'how much the interest rate caused that is still argued' (C2-H08).
Changed: dropped 'output fell by around a fifth'. It is one estimate (Mitchell, Solomou and Weale) and it cluttered the numbers.

Changed: page 2 now says 'nearly eight million tons', so the on-screen 8 MILLION TONS matches what is spoken. It also adds that historians still argue how much was money and how much was shortage (C2-H03 is medium confidence, and the weight of causes is contested).

Changed: 'the government was buying most food' became 'controlled almost all food' (C2-H05: controls covered over 94% of foodstuffs). 'Shared, not bid up' is the film's explanation, not a source quote, and is kept short.
Changed: page 6 now adds the central banks' view right after Mattei's, that lost jobs are a cost, not the goal (C2-M17), so her reading is clearly hers.

Changed: removed Mattei's 'same pattern today' (C2-H19) from the New Zealand pages. She was speaking about the US and Europe, and keeping it there risked implying she said it about New Zealand. It also saved words.
Changed: on page 10, 'the limit isn't money, it's workers, materials and machines' is now credited to 'economists who study how modern money works' (C2-M12), not said as a plain fact.

Changed: dropped 'the Reserve Bank is raising rates again, with unemployment at a ten-year high' and the 'mostly fuel' framing from the ending. Both read as partisan a month before the 7 November election (C2-M18 notes the Bank gives wider reasons). The ending keeps only the released figures, 4.1% and 2.9%.
Changed: page 8's 'petrol up a third, building a new house up nearly a fifth' was cut. The page was over 30 seconds, and two pages over the time limit were merged into one.

Changed: the numbers on screen now match the spoken words. 2 IN 100 → 1 IN 10 replaces 11 IN 100, and 200,000 BUILT replaces 213,000. The dropped 9 DAYS and PAY CUT cards were replaced with words that are actually said.

Changed (one plain name per thing): synonyms removed. 'Bank credit' and 'minting' became 'new money'. 'Rate jump', 'rate rise' and 'rate' became 'interest rate'. 'The crash' and 'the slump' are no longer spoken (the slump is only a page name). 'The experts' cure' became 'the cure'. 'Government bonds' and 'IOUs' became 'government debt'.

Replaced 'machines start' with smoke sliding out and goods popping up, so nothing moves like a cartoon. Raised the fal estimate from US$0.75 to about US$1.75 to allow for about three tries per painting.

Still open: length. The script is about 580 words, or about 4 minutes 5 seconds at Malina's pace, and spoken numbers like 'nineteen twenty' add words. Pages 7, 8 and 9 are each close to 30 seconds. A script pass should trim about 20-30 words, for example the 'today's Bank of England governor' clause or the 'how much from the world' line.

Still open: unemployment 3.2% to 5.6% spans the 2021-23 rate rises, the cuts of 2024-25 and the new 2026 rises (C2-N10, C2-N11, C2-N12). 'Has climbed' is true, but viewers may read all of it as caused by the first round of rate rises. The 2023 shrinkings also involved cyclones.

Still open: 'same kind of cure' is a comparison. In 1920s Britain the cure also meant spending cuts and gold; in New Zealand only the interest rate is shown. The review was commissioned by the current government and its timing was questioned (C2-N15).

Still open: house prices aren't in the 7.3% (C2-N08). The narration keeps them in separate sentences, but viewers may merge them. 'You can't quickly make more land' is the film's point, not the Royal Commission's.

Still open: the link from gold to the coal wage cuts is the standard account, but coal had other troubles too (C2-H13). The Bank of England governor's 2025 view (C2-H12) supports only the claim that the pound was set too high, not Mattei's reading.

Still open: the sources (C2-H04, C2-H05) were read only in search summaries or from a single encyclopedic source. Recheck the rent strike (estimates run from 20,000 to 25,000 households) and the food-control details before recording.

Still open: page 10's 'cost of building a new house' and the tradables split from the world are no longer spoken. Cost-push from fuel is touched on only through '2.9% without fuel', so this angle still teaches less about other causes (costs, expectations, profits) than a mechanism-first outline would.

draft.title: Four price tags
draft.pitch: The politician from chapter 1 says creating money causes inflation, so the film tests that claim on four real price stories: Germany 1923, Japan's decade of money creation, the 1973 oil shock and New Zealand 2022. A fifth case comes back from chapter 1's own war. Each case ends on a verdict card (the money, a shortage, or who spent it on what), and the verdicts build the rule. The viewer comes away knowing that it isn't whether money is created that matters. It's where and how it's spent. The film also shows the honest edge, why the official story still blames the money, and who pays for the cure.
draft.the_one_idea: Creating money only pushes prices up when the spending chases things the economy can't make more of, so where and how it is spent matters more than how much is created.
draft.how_it_explains_inflation_through_chapte: It opens on chapter 1's last scene: the same politician at the lectern with his paper jaw, the stack of money and the growing price tag. It turns his claim into the question each case has to answer. The verdict card reuses chapter 1's blank price tag and pay packet. The fifth case is chapter 1's own 1915 shell factory. Prices roughly doubled there while almost everyone had a job, which is chapter 1's line "it can run out of workers, materials and machines" made concrete. Page 9 goes back to chapter 1's experts and their card NO NEW MONEY, and shows the cure Britain was already using (a 7% interest rate, mass unemployment). Mattei's reading is said as hers, as in chapter 1. Page 10 brings it home to New Zealand now with chapter 1's dole queue and iron weight, and ends on chapter 1's "Sound familiar?" rhythm plus a hook for chapter 3.
draft.honest_edge: It is said in three places. In Germany 1923 the verdict is "yes, the money... but money paid for nothing being made" (C2-C02, C2-C03). New Zealand 2022's verdict is "both", and it says plainly that part came from spending chasing too few builders and houses and that nobody has split it up (C2-N02, C2-N08, C2-N16, C2-N15). Page 7 is the core: the honest edge gets a verdict card of its own. In chapter 1's war, prices roughly doubled when almost everyone had a job and goods were being sunk, so spending chasing things the economy couldn't make more of pushed prices up (C2-H01, C2-H02, C2-H03). The oil verdict also admits that America's central bank says its own loose money helped the rise spread (C2-C14).

pages.name: The claim
pages.what_is_said: Picks up chapter 1's last line. Inflation means prices, in general, going up over time. The politician's answer: create money and the price tag grows. We test it on real price tags, asking one question each time: the money, a shortage, or who spent it on what?
pages.sample_line: So let's test it... four real price tags, and the same question each time.
pages.on_screen: Chapter 1's parliament with the politician; his jaw moves on 'create money, and the price tag grows'. The stack of money and the price tag from chapter 1 grow side by side. On 'four real price tags' four blank tags flip up in a row. On 'the money? a shortage? or who spent it' a blank verdict card slides in with three boxes.
new_paintings: verdict card (small: blank paper card with three tick boxes)

pages.name: Case one: Germany 1923
pages.what_is_said: The case everyone points to. In January 1923 French and Belgian soldiers marched into the Ruhr, Germany's coal and steel heartland. The government told workers to down tools and kept paying them with newly created money. Prices were already racing; this sent them through the roof. By November one American dollar cost more than four trillion marks. Verdict: yes, the money, but money paid for nothing being made.
pages.sample_line: verdict? yes, the money... but money paid for nothing being made.
pages.on_screen: Chapter 1's pithead with its wheel stopped. Soldiers slide in on 'marched into the Ruhr'. A printing press flips up on 'newly created money' and spits notes into a wheelbarrow; a loaf of bread's price tag spins up. The verdict card stamps MONEY + NOTHING MADE.
new_paintings: French and Belgian soldiers, 1923 (big figure; chapter 1's soldiers are British and in the wrong uniform)

pages.name: Case two: Japan
pages.what_is_said: In 2013 Japan's central bank set out to double the money it had created, within two years, then kept going. If creating money causes inflation, prices should soar. They barely moved: about half a percent a year for nearly a decade. Verdict: not the money. Most economists say much of it sat in the banks and never reached the shops.
pages.sample_line: if creating money causes inflation, prices should soar... they barely moved.
pages.on_screen: A painted Tokyo noodle shop counter. A stack of yen notes grows taller on 'double' and 'kept going', while the price tag on a bowl of noodles stays still and wobbles slightly. On 'sat in the banks' the stack slides into chapter 1's bank object. The verdict card stamps NOT THE MONEY.

pages.name: Case three: oil 1973
pages.what_is_said: In 1973 the price of oil nearly quadrupled in three months; in 1979 it more than doubled again. Everything that needs fuel to make or move got dearer, and American prices were soon rising almost fifteen percent a year. Verdict: a shortage started it. But America's own central bank says its loose money helped the rise spread.
pages.sample_line: verdict? a shortage started it... but america's own central bank says its loose money helped it spread.
pages.on_screen: A 1970s petrol station with a queue of cars. An oil barrel's price tag flips from $2.90 to $11.65. On 'make or move' a row of small price tags tips up like dominoes (basket, bread, locomotive). The verdict card stamps SHORTAGE, then a smaller tag drops in: + LOOSE MONEY.
new_paintings: 1970s petrol station with queue of cars (background)

pages.name: Case four: New Zealand 2022, what rose
pages.what_is_said: Case four is ours. By mid-2022 New Zealand prices were rising 7.3 percent a year, the fastest in thirty-two years. Petrol was up about a third, the cost of building a new house nearly a fifth. In 2020 and 2021 the Reserve Bank created money to buy about fifty-three billion dollars of government bonds, and house prices jumped about thirty percent in a year.
