strengths: A clear, repeatable form: each case is a small mystery with a verdict, so the viewer predicts and checks. That is Pinker's 'concrete case before each idea', and the rule on page 8 is built only from cases already shown.

It answers the user's point head-on ('it depends on where and how the money is spent') with evidence for and against, not assertion. Japan is the strongest single counter-example to 'money = inflation'.

The honest edge isn't buried. It gets its own verdict card, and it uses chapter 1's own shell factory, so the series stays consistent: 'it can run out of workers, materials and machines' turns from a slogan into a case.
It ties tightly to chapter 1: the same politician, price tag, pay packet, experts' NO NEW MONEY card, iron weight and dole queue, and it ends on the 'Sound familiar?' rhythm.
The New Zealand case is local, recent and candid ('nobody has split it up'), and the ending connects to the Reserve Bank raising rates now.

weaknesses_and_risks: Length is tight. Five cases plus the rule plus the cure plus now come to about 560 words, roughly 4 minutes at Malina's 140 words a minute. Pages 5 and 10 run near 30 seconds. If it runs long, drop Japan's 'then kept going' and the oil 1979 clause, or cut the war case into the rule page.
The title promises four price tags but delivers five (the war is a 'one more' twist). Some viewers may find that a cheat. It could be retitled, or Japan and oil merged.

Germany 1923: inflation was already high in 1922, before the Ruhr, and historians disagree about how much reparations caused it (C2-C01, C2-C02). The verdict 'money paid for nothing being made' fits 1923 but simplifies the whole episode. No figure for the fall in German output was found, so the narration can only say output fell, not by how much.

Japan: the reason prices didn't rise is contested. 'Sat in the banks' is the mainstream explanation of where the money went (C2-C06, C2-C09). Ageing, expectations and weak demand are other causes, and monetarists say prices would have fallen without it. The 0.5% average includes the 2014 consumption tax rise.

Oil: the Fed's own history says the Great Inflation began before the oil shocks and blames loose money (C2-C14). The verdict 'a shortage started it' is fair for the 1973 jump but not for the whole decade. The narration hedges with '+ loose money', but critics could still call it cherry-picked.

New Zealand 2022: no published split exists (C2-N16), so the verdict 'both' is a judgement. House prices are not in the CPI (C2-N08), so putting houses next to the 7.3% could mislead unless the narration keeps them separate. How much the Reserve Bank's money creation raised house prices is unquantified.

Page 7: wartime British price figures are reconstructed annual averages (C2-H01). The war-finance detail rests on an NBER chapter seen only in a search summary (C2-H03, medium confidence). Submarines and shipping losses are a simplification of the causes.

Page 9 chronology: the Brussels experts met in September 1920, after the April 1920 rate rise, so the narration must say the cure 'had already begun', not that the experts caused it. Whether the rate rise caused the 1920-21 slump or deepened one already coming is debated (C2-H08).

Page 10: the link between New Zealand's rate rises and unemployment rising to 5.6% by 2026 is the mainstream mechanism, but rates were also cut in 2024-25, and the 2023 recessions involved cyclones (C2-N11). 'Mostly fuel' is the film's framing; the Reserve Bank cites core inflation and expectations (C2-M18). With the election on 7 November, the tone must stay neutral and name no party.

New paintings are needed for 1923 French and Belgian soldiers (uniform accuracy, no flags or insignia that mislead), a Tokyo shop (cultural accuracy) and a 1970s petrol queue. Each needs a history check before use.

The cure-and-power ending (pages 9-10) leans on Mattei, and the hook 'what else can stop prices rising' promises a chapter 3 on alternative tools (C2-M13: taxes, buffer stocks, price caps) that the user hasn't yet agreed to.

The viewer comes away knowing that whether money is created matters less than where and how it is spent. They also see the honest edge, and what the cure for blaming the money costs, then and now.
